1.overview:
After Moses dies, the LORD speaks to Joshua: cross the Jordan with the people into the land he is giving them, from the wilderness and Lebanon to the Euphrates. He promises to be with Joshua as he was with Moses, and three times tells him to be strong and of a good courage, keeping the book of the law in his mouth day and night. Joshua tells the officers to have the people prepare food, for in three days they will cross. Then he reminds Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh of their promise to Moses: their fighting men must cross ahead of their brothers. They answer that they will obey Joshua as they obeyed Moses.

Notice who speaks last. The LORD's charge, “be strong and of a good courage,” comes three times in vv. 6–9, and the eastern tribes close the chapter with the same words (v. 18). The people hand the LORD's encouragement back to their new leader.

1.hermeneutics:
Egyptian kings were told that their god had put the nations under their feet. In the Hymn of Victory carved at Karnak for Thutmose III (15th century BC), Amun says he has felled the king's enemies “beneath thy sandals,” that the king tramples all countries, and that he has crossed the Great Bend of Naharin, the Euphrates. Verses 3–5 use the same picture: every place the sole of the foot treads, out to “the great river,” and no one able to stand. What changes is who receives the land. The promise is spoken to Joshua, but “your foot” in v. 3 is plural, the whole people's, and Joshua's task is to divide the land among them (v. 6).

“All the land of the Hittites” (v. 4) sounds odd for Canaan. In the 14th and 13th centuries BC the Hittite empire ruled Syria, and Assyrian scribes later kept the name for the whole west. Sennacherib describes his campaign of 701 BC against Sidon, the Philistine cities, and Hezekiah of Judah as a march against “the Hittite-land.” For readers in the time of the kings, the phrase named the country between the Euphrates and the sea.

Hammurabi (18th century BC) ended his laws by addressing the kings who would come after him. A future king was to keep the words written on the stela, not alter them, and judge by them; if he did, Shamash would lengthen his reign. Verses 7–8 set Joshua the same terms as a successor: keep all the law Moses commanded, turn neither right nor left, and you will prosper. Hammurabi's successor answers to Hammurabi. Joshua's law comes through Moses, and the promise of success comes from the LORD, who also tells him to keep the book in his mouth day and night.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence through four speeches, each handing authority one step further down.
notes: **Be strong:** the pair “be strong and of a good courage” (Hebrew *chazaq* and *amats*) comes 4 times. The LORD says it three times (vv. 6, 7, 9) and the people say it last (v. 18).
**Moses:** though dead, he is named 11 times in 18 verses, five of them as “servant” of the LORD (vv. 1, 2, 7, 13, 15). His law, his word, and the land he gave frame every speech.
**Whithersoever:** the LORD's promise “whithersoever thou goest” (vv. 7, 9) comes back in the tribes' pledge, “whithersoever thou sendest us” (v. 16).

Chapter 1 opens the book and its first section, the entry into the land (chapters 1–5). Its first words, “after the death of Moses,” join it to the end of Deuteronomy (34:5–9), and the three days of v. 11 start the count that runs to the crossing (3:2). The speech to the eastern tribes opens a thread that closes in 22:1–6, when Joshua sends them home to their rest.
**Backward and forward:** the charge to be strong repeats Moses' words to Joshua (Deuteronomy 31:7, 23). Judges opens the same way, “after the death of Joshua” (Judges 1:1).

traditions.text: The Church's footnote to v. 5, where the LORD promises to be with Joshua as he was with Moses, points to the revelation on priesthood. There the President of the High Priesthood is to preside over the whole church “and to be like unto Moses,” a seer, revelator, translator, and prophet. The cross-reference sets Joshua's succession beside the office that, in Latter-day Saint teaching, carries Moses' role forward.

traditions.date: c. 124 BC; c. 400 BC (Book of Mormon)
traditions.text: The footnote to the promise of prosperity in v. 7 gathers the Book of Mormon's refrain about prospering in the land. King Benjamin tells his sons to search the records diligently and keep the commandments, “that ye may prosper in the land,” and Jarom reports the promise kept in war. Benjamin ties a written record to the people's prosperity, as vv. 7–8 tie the book of the law to Joshua's success.

The footnote to v. 9, where the LORD is with Joshua wherever he goes, points to D&C 38:7, in which the Lord tells the Saints he is in their midst though they cannot see him. A later revelation to elders sent out to preach repeats Joshua's charge almost word for word, telling them to be of good cheer and not to fear, “for I the Lord am with you.” The second passage is a thematic link, not a footnote.

Josephus has Joshua send spies to Jericho at once and call the leaders of Reuben, Gad, and half Manasseh, urging them to keep their promise for the sake of Moses, who never wearied of caring for them even as he died. He gives the number of eastern fighting men who followed as fifty thousand, where Joshua 4:13 says about forty thousand crossed. The march, he adds, went from Abila to the Jordan, sixty furlongs.

This Jewish retelling of biblical history opens its Joshua story with God rebuking him for mourning and hoping in vain that Moses still lived. God tells him, “Take the garments of his wisdom,” and to gird himself with the girdle of Moses' knowledge, and he will become another man. When Joshua puts them on, his mind is kindled, and he warns the captains that the former generation died for speaking against God. The scene turns the succession of vv. 1–9 into a change of clothing, as with Elijah's mantle passing to Elisha.

A baraita uses this chapter to date Moses' death. Israel came up out of the Jordan on the tenth of the first month (4:19); subtract the three days of v. 11 and the thirty days of mourning, and Moses died on the seventh of Adar. Rashi, on 2:1, draws the consequence that Joshua must have sent the spies while the mourning was still going on.

Rav Yehuda reports that three thousand laws were forgotten during the mourning for Moses. When the people asked Joshua to recover them from heaven, he answered from Deuteronomy 30:12 that the Torah is not in heaven. In another version the people rose against him, and God told him to occupy them with war, reading v. 2, “arise, go over this Jordan,” as that command.

The rabbis ask what v. 8 requires. Rabbi Ami says a chapter of Mishnah morning and evening fulfills it; Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai says even the Shema morning and evening. When Ben Dama, who had learned all the Torah, asked whether he might study Greek wisdom, Rabbi Yishmael quoted v. 8 and told him to find an hour that is neither day nor night. Rabbi Yonatan disagreed: the verse is a blessing, given because Joshua never left the tent (Exodus 33:11).

Verse 18 makes rebellion against Joshua's word a capital crime, and the Talmud uses it to judge Joab's killing of Amasa. Amasa had delayed mustering Judah for David because he found the men studying Torah, and he read the closing word “only” as a limit on a king's power. Solomon accepts the reading: a ruler's command does not override the study of Torah.

Stephen's speech recalls the tabernacle that the fathers “brought in with Jesus” into the land of the nations. KJV gives Joshua's name here in its Greek form, *Iesous*, which is also the name of Jesus; Hebrew *Yehoshua* lies behind both. Hebrews 4:8 does the same.

Arguing with Jewish opponents, Tertullian notes that Oshea son of Nun was renamed Jesus when he was being prepared to succeed Moses. He reads the change as a figure: the people entered the land of promise not through Moses, “the Law's discipline,” but through Joshua, the new law's grace. The death of Moses in v. 2 thus becomes the point where the law hands over to grace. Justin Martyr had read Joshua's name the same way a generation earlier.

2.overview:
Joshua sends two men from Shittim to spy out Jericho, and they lodge in the house of Rahab, a harlot whose house is built into the town wall. When the king demands them, she hides them under flax on her roof and sends the searchers off toward the Jordan fords. She tells the spies what Jericho has heard of the Red Sea and of Sihon and Og, confesses the LORD as God in heaven and on earth, and asks them to swear to spare her family. A scarlet line in her window will mark the house. She lets them down the wall by a cord, and after three days in the mountain they report to Joshua.

Notice whose words the spies bring home. Their report in v. 24 repeats Rahab's confession from v. 9: the LORD has given the land, and its people faint with fear. The news that matters comes from a Canaanite woman.

2.hermeneutics:
Hammurabi's laws (18th century BC) give several rulings about women who kept taverns, and one makes the tavern a place a king watched. If conspirators meet in a tavern-keeper's house and she does not seize them and deliver them to the court, she is to be put to death (§109). A house where strangers could eat and lodge without question was where news and plots passed, and Jericho's king sends there first (v. 3). By the standards of her own world, Rahab's choice to hide the men is treason against her king, carrying the penalty she fears for herself and all her family (vv. 12–13).

Treaties of the period protected households by oath and named a sign of the bond. When Ramesses II and the Hittite king Hattusili III made peace (c. 1259 BC), the text on its silver tablet promises that whoever broke its terms would see his house, land, and subjects desolated, while whoever kept them would be preserved with his household and his land. Rahab's agreement with the spies has the parts of such a pact on a small scale: an oath, a token (v. 12), protection for her father's house, and a clause placing blood guilt on whoever breaks the terms (v. 19). The parties are unequal. A Canaanite woman asks to be bound into an oath sworn “by the LORD,” the God of the invaders, whom she has just confessed in the words of Deuteronomy 4:39 as God “in heaven above, and in earth beneath” (v. 11).

rows.text: Back to Joshua with her words

notes: **Echo:** v. 24 takes three pieces from v. 9: the LORD has given “the land,” “all the inhabitants” of the land, and they “faint” (the same Hebrew verb, *namogu*, both times).
**Kindness and oath:** *chesed* (KJV “kindness,” “kindly”) comes 3 times (vv. 12 twice, 14), and the verb “swear” 3 times (vv. 12, 17, 20). The bargain is told in the language of covenant.
**Line of hope:** the “line” of scarlet thread (vv. 18, 21) is *tikvah*, the ordinary Hebrew word for “hope.” The cord she lets them down by in v. 15 is a different word.

Chapter 2 runs alongside the preparations of chapter 1. Joshua's three days (1:11) and the spies' three days in the mountain (v. 22) overlap, and the camp moves only in 3:1. Rahab's story is left open here and finished after the walls fall, when the same two men bring out her household (6:22–25).

**Backward and forward:** Joshua's two spies recall the twelve Moses sent from Kadesh (Numbers 13). Rahab's report answers the Song of the Sea, which foretold that “all the inhabitants of Canaan shall melt away” (Exodus 15:15).

traditions.text: The JST changes one word in v. 5, where Rahab tells the king's men she does not know where the spies went: the archaic “wot” becomes “know.” Her answer, and the rest of the chapter, otherwise stand as written. It is the only JST change the Church's footnotes record in Joshua 1–5.

The footnote to the spies' report in v. 24 points to Nephi's account of the conquest. Nephi says the people of Canaan were driven out because they had rejected every word of God and were ripe in iniquity, and he states the rule behind it: “the Lord esteemeth all flesh in one.” The one who is righteous is favored of God. Read beside this chapter, Rahab is a Canaanite on the favored side of that rule; the link to her is thematic.

In Josephus the spies first walk around Jericho unnoticed, taken for curious strangers, and note which parts of the walls and which gates are weak. At evening they sup at an inn near the wall “kept by Rahab,” and the king wants them brought in to be examined by torture. Josephus adds that Joshua reported the oath to Eleazar the high priest and the senate, who confirmed it.

The Aramaic Targum renders the Hebrew for “harlot” as “innkeeper,” the reading Josephus also follows. Rashi accepts it and explains that she sold provisions. On “secretly” in v. 1, whose Hebrew letters can also spell “deaf” or “pottery,” he offers two pictures: Joshua told the spies to act deaf so people would talk freely before them, or to carry pots and pass as potters.
traditions.cite: Targum Jonathan on Joshua 2:1; Rashi on Joshua 2:1

traditions.text: Verse 4 says Rahab “hid them” with a singular pronoun in Hebrew. Rashi suggests she crammed both into a space meant for one, then reports the Tanchuma's answer: the two spies were Phinehas and Caleb, and Phinehas needed no hiding, since like an angel he could not be seen. Pseudo-Philo names the spies differently, as Caleb's sons (see chapter 6).

A baraita counts eight prophets who were also priests among Rahab's descendants, Jeremiah and Baruch among them, and Rabbi Yehuda adds the prophetess Huldah. The link is a word: Huldah's husband descends from Tikvah (2 Kings 22:14), and Rahab's scarlet line is *tikvah*. Rav Nahman reconciles this with a tradition tracing Huldah to Joshua by saying that Rahab converted and married Joshua, who had daughters but no sons.

The rabbis ask how Rahab knew that Jericho's men had lost all courage (v. 11), and answer that every prince and ruler of the land had been her client. They give her a history: ten years old at the Exodus, a harlot through all forty years in the wilderness, a convert at fifty when the spies came. She prays that her sins be forgiven for the sake of the rope, the window, and the flax by which she saved them.

Two New Testament letters cite Rahab for different lessons. Hebrews lists her among the heroes of faith: “By faith the harlot Rahab perished not” with the unbelievers. James uses the same scene to show that faith works: she was justified when she received the messengers and sent them out another way.

Matthew's genealogy of Jesus names “Rachab” as the wife of Salmon and mother of Boaz, one of four women in the list. The Old Testament never gives Salmon a wife (Ruth 4:21), and this marriage appears nowhere else. The rabbis, by contrast, married her to Joshua.

Writing from Rome to Corinth, Clement says Rahab was saved for her faith and her hospitality. He retells the chapter closely, flax and all, and reads the scarlet thread as a sign that redemption would flow through the blood of the Lord to all who believe. His conclusion: there was “not only faith, but prophecy, in this woman.”

Justin sets the scarlet thread beside the Passover blood on the doors in Egypt. Both, he tells Trypho, announced salvation through the blood of Christ, by which people out of all nations who were once harlots and unrighteous receive remission of sins. Rahab's own past becomes part of the sign.

Irenaeus has Rahab receive “three spies,” though the text says two, and reads them as a figure of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. A Gentile who condemned herself as a sinner, she was preserved with all her house through faith in the scarlet sign when the city fell. He links her to Jesus' saying that publicans and harlots enter the kingdom first (Matthew 21:31).

traditions.source: Theodosius, On the Topography of the Holy Land
traditions.text: Christian pilgrims were shown Rahab's house. Theodosius, who wrote a short guide for pilgrims, places it at the Fountain of Elisha, two miles from Jericho, and calls it the house of Rahab the harlot “who took in the spies.” In the same passage he puts Gilgal and its twelve stones a mile from Jericho.

3.overview:
Israel leaves Shittim and camps by the Jordan. After three days the officers give the order: when the priests carry the ark of the covenant, the people are to follow it, keeping about two thousand cubits back. Joshua tells the people to sanctify themselves, and the LORD promises to begin magnifying Joshua as he did Moses. Joshua announces the sign: when the priests' feet rest in the water, the river will be cut off and stand in a heap. The Jordan is in flood, yet as the priests step in, the water stops far upstream at the city of Adam, and the people cross on dry ground while the priests stand in the riverbed.

The ark leads. It is named ten times in seventeen verses, and the people keep their distance from it so “that ye may know the way” (v. 4). The water does not part until the priests' feet are already wet.

3.hermeneutics:
The Jordan can stop. In 1266 the Mamluk sultan Baybars ordered a bridge built over the river near Damiya, the site usually identified with the city Adam of v. 16. The Arab historian al-Nuwairi (14th century) records that when part of the piers gave way, the workmen could not repair them against the high water, until in the night before 8 December 1267 the river ceased to flow. Riders sent upstream found that a lofty bank on the west side had fallen into the river and dammed it. The water was held from midnight until the fourth hour of the day, long enough to repair the piers in the dry bed by firelight. Nuwairi claims no miracle. Verse 16 places the heap of water at the same stretch of river, “very far” from where Israel crossed. What the text stresses is the timing: the water stops at the moment the priests' feet dip into it (v. 15), as Joshua had said it would (v. 13).

Assyrian kings boasted of crossing rivers in flood. Shalmaneser III (9th century BC) says more than once that he crossed the Euphrates “at its flood,” in one account in boats of goatskin. When Ashurbanipal's troops were afraid to cross the Idide, a raging torrent in Elam, Ishtar of Arbela spoke to the army in a dream: “I will go before Assurbanipal.” The soldiers trusted the dream and crossed in safety. Joshua 3 has the same pieces: a river over its banks (v. 15), a people who have never passed this way (v. 4), and a divine presence going first. The presence is the ark itself, carried by priests into the water ahead of everyone, and the people walk over without boats.

notes: **Word, then deed:** vv. 14–17 carry out vv. 8 and 13 in nearly the same words: the feet of the priests, the waters “cut off,” the waters that “came down from above,” standing in “an heap” (Hebrew *ned*, vv. 13, 16).
**Pass over:** the verb *avar* runs through the crossing story, 9 times in chapter 3 and 13 in chapter 4.
**The ark:** named 10 times, often with a title: “the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God” (v. 3), “the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth” (v. 11).

Chapters 3–4 form one account. Chapter 3 tells the crossing through to the last person on the far bank; chapter 4 goes back over the same hours to tell of the stones and the priests' coming up. The three days announced in 1:11 run out here (v. 2), and the camp at Gilgal begins in 4:19.

**Backward and forward:** the heap of water echoes the Song of the Sea, where the floods “stood upright as an heap” (Exodus 15:8). Elijah and Elisha later part the same river near Jericho (2 Kings 2:8, 14).

traditions.text: Rebuking his brothers, Nephi retells Israel's story and moves from the wilderness straight to this river: “after they had crossed the river Jordan” the Lord made them mighty to drive out the people of the land. In the verses before, he insists that all of it was done “by his word.” Nephi keeps the order of Joshua 3: the crossing comes first, the conquest after.

The Church's footnote to v. 4, where Israel must follow the ark because “ye have not passed this way heretofore,” points to the Liahona. Lehi finds a brass ball at his tent door with a spindle that “pointed the way” into the wilderness. In both stories a people in unknown country follow a sacred object the Lord has given.

For Joshua's command in v. 5, “Sanctify yourselves: for to morrow the LORD will do wonders,” the footnote points to a revelation to the elders in Kirtland. They too are told to sanctify themselves, with the promise that they will be endowed with power. Both passages make holiness the preparation for an act of God.

Josephus explains Joshua's worry: the current was strong, no bridge had ever been laid over the Jordan, and Israel had no ferry boats. He sets the order of march: priests with the ark, Levites carrying the tabernacle and its vessels, then the tribes with wives and children in the middle, so the stream would not sweep them away. In his account the river becomes fordable, with the sand showing on the bottom.

The Tosefta notices two changes from the wilderness march. On other days the ark traveled behind the standards of Judah and Reuben; on this day it went in front, as v. 11 says. On other days Levites carried it; on this day priests did. Rabbi Yosei counts this as one of three occasions when priests carried the ark, with Jericho (6:6) and Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:6).

How high was the heap? Rabbi Yehuda says twelve mil by twelve, the size of Israel's camp. Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon answers that water moves faster than people, so the water rose in heaps upon heaps more than three hundred mil high, until all the kings east and west saw it, which is why their hearts melted (5:1). While still in the riverbed, the Talmud adds, Joshua warned Israel that if they did not drive out the land's inhabitants, the waters would come back and drown them and him.

Why two thousand cubits (v. 4)? Following Midrash Tanchuma, Rashi says it was the distance a person may walk on the Sabbath, so that the people could go and pray before the ark; Joshua knew they would be besieging Jericho on a Sabbath. He also reports a reading that two arks traveled together, the ark of the Presence and the coffin holding Joseph's bones.

The Aramaic Targum softens the language of God's presence. Where v. 7 has the LORD promise to be with Joshua as he was with Moses, the Targum says his Memra, his Word, will be at Joshua's aid as it was at Moses'. In v. 10, the living God being “among you” becomes God being pleased to make his Shechinah dwell among them. The ark is the sign of that dwelling presence.

Teaching the newly baptized in Milan, Ambrose lists cases where grace overruled nature: the Red Sea hardening into walls, the rock giving water, the iron axe head floating. Among them is the Jordan, which “returned, contrary to nature, to the source of its stream.” His point is that if a prophet's word could change nature, Christ's word can change the bread and wine of the Eucharist.

In lectures for candidates preparing for baptism, Cyril calls Joshua a type of Jesus, whose name he bore. Joshua began to rule over the people at the Jordan, where Christ began to preach after he was baptized. Joshua appointed twelve to divide the inheritance, and Jesus sent out twelve apostles.

Jerome's memorial of his friend Paula describes her pilgrimage. After a night at Jericho she hurried to the Jordan, stood on the bank at sunrise, and recalled how the priests' feet stood firm in the middle of the riverbed (v. 17), how the waters later parted for Elijah and Elisha, and how the Lord cleansed the waters by his baptism. For pilgrims the river held all three crossings at once.

4.overview:
Once all Israel has crossed, the LORD has Joshua choose one man from each tribe to carry a stone from the riverbed, where the priests are standing, to the night's camp. Joshua also sets up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan. The armed men of the eastern tribes, about forty thousand, cross ahead of the rest, and the LORD magnifies Joshua as he did Moses. When the priests come up with the ark, the river returns and floods its banks again. On the tenth day of the first month Israel camps at Gilgal, and Joshua sets up the stones there.

The stones are made for questions. Twice the chapter imagines a child asking what the stones mean (vv. 6, 21), and twice it supplies the answer a parent should give. The memorial works only if someone asks and someone remembers.

4.hermeneutics:
Kings marked hard crossings with monuments to themselves. At the Nahr el-Kalb, the Dog River north of Beirut, where the coast road crosses the river, Ramesses II had stelae cut into the rock during his campaigns in the 13th century BC, one dated to his fourth year. In 671 BC Esarhaddon, after his conquest of Egypt, carved his own stela beside one of them, and later rulers kept adding theirs. Each bears a king's name and a record of his victories. The twelve stones of vv. 3–9 and 20 mark Israel's crossing at a river too, but carry no name and no inscription. Twelve ordinary men carry them, one for each tribe, and their meaning is kept in the answer parents give their children (vv. 6–7, 21–24).

Egyptian kings made sure their victories were known in every part of the land. Ramesses II had his account of the battle of Kadesh (c. 1274 BC) carved on the walls of his temples at Abydos, at Thebes three times, at Derr, and at Abu Simbel. Verse 24 gives the crossing the same purpose with a different subject: all the people of the earth are to know “the hand of the LORD, that it is mighty.” The chapter does say that the LORD magnified Joshua that day (v. 14), yet both answers to the children's question tell what the LORD did. Joshua's name is not in them.

notes: **Two answers:** the first answer points to the ark (v. 7). The second points back to the Red Sea and out to “all the people of the earth” (vv. 23–24).
**Pass over:** *avar* comes 13 times, and “stones” 8 times (vv. 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 20, 21).
**Two sets of stones:** v. 9 places twelve stones in the riverbed besides the twelve carried to Gilgal (v. 20). The doubling puzzled early readers (see Traditions).

The crossing account of 3:1–4:24 ends with the camp at Gilgal and a date, the tenth of the first month (v. 19), which looks ahead to the Passover there on the fourteenth (5:10). Gilgal becomes Israel's base for the campaigns that follow (9:6; 10:6; 14:6).

**Backward and forward:** the children's question echoes the Passover's “What mean ye by this service?” (Exodus 12:26) and Deuteronomy 6:20. Elijah later builds an altar of twelve stones, one for each tribe (1 Kings 18:31).

traditions.text: A thematic link to vv. 21–24, where fathers tell their children what the LORD did. Alma, charging his son Helaman, rehearses how God brought the fathers out of Egypt, through the Red Sea, and “by his power into the promised land.” Then he turns it into a duty: he has always kept their captivity in remembrance, and his son ought to do the same. As at Gilgal, the deliverance is handed down from father to son.

A thematic link to the purpose clause of vv. 6–7. Nephi explains why his people talk, preach, and write of Christ: “that our children may know” where to look for a remission of their sins. The stones of Gilgal and Nephi's record are both made for a coming generation who will ask what they mean.

The rabbis took the stones as real objects with a real weight. Rabbi Yehuda reports that three sages once stood on the stones from the Jordan, measured them, and found each weighed about forty seah. From that, and the rule that a man can lift onto his own shoulder a third of what others can load on him, they worked out the weight of the spies' cluster of grapes (Numbers 13:23). They also read “where ye shall lodge this night” (v. 3) as limiting the command to that one night.

The date in v. 19 became evidence in a legal question: may an uncircumcised man be sprinkled with the water that cleanses from contact with the dead? Rabbi Yohanan argues yes. Israel came up from the Jordan on the tenth, and to keep Passover in purity on the fourteenth, its first sprinkling had to come by the tenth, when the wilderness generation was still uncircumcised (5:2–8). The Talmud adds that they were not circumcised on the tenth itself because they were weary from the journey.

The Talmud counts three sets of stones. Moses set up one in Moab, which it infers by linking the “declare” of Deuteronomy 1:5 with the “very plainly” of 27:8. Joshua set one in the middle of the Jordan (v. 9) and one at Gilgal (v. 20). The doubling of vv. 9 and 20 thus becomes part of a larger pattern.

Verse 11 says the ark passed over after all the people, “and the priests,” in their sight. The Talmud pictures the priests left on the east bank once the waters returned, and the ark lifting its bearers and carrying them across. It uses the scene against Uzzah, who reached out to steady the ark (2 Samuel 6:6–7): an ark that once carried its bearers did not need his hand.

Linking this chapter to Deuteronomy 27, the Talmud crowds a day of miracles into the crossing. Israel went on to Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, more than sixty mil away, built the altar, wrote the Torah on the stones in seventy languages, pronounced the blessings and curses, and then took the stones and came back to sleep at Gilgal, “where ye shall lodge this night.” Rashi repeats this account on v. 3, and on v. 9 insists that the stones set in the riverbed were a second set.

Josephus has Israel go fifty furlongs past the river and camp ten furlongs from Jericho. There Joshua builds an altar from the stones the heads of the tribes had taken out of the deep, as a memorial of the river's division, and offers sacrifice on it. In Josephus the memorial stones become an altar, which Joshua 4 never says.

In a sermon on the baptism of Christ, Gregory reads Israel's history as a series of figures of baptism. The people did not enter the land of promise until Joshua guided them through the Jordan, and Joshua, who set up twelve stones in the stream, was anticipating “the twelve disciples, the ministers of Baptism.” Jerome's account of Paula's pilgrimage likewise takes the stones as the twelve apostles.
traditions.cite: On the Baptism of Christ; Jerome, Letter 108.12

traditions.text: Eusebius' gazetteer of biblical places says that at the second mile from Jericho the stones brought up out of the Jordan were still pointed out in his day. Two centuries later the pilgrim guide of Theodosius puts Gilgal a mile from Jericho and lists among its sights the twelve stones “lifted out of the Jordan.” The phrase “unto this day” in v. 9 was still being claimed for the stones in late antiquity.

5.overview:
The kings west of the Jordan lose heart when they hear of the crossing. At that time the LORD tells Joshua to make flint knives and circumcise Israel again: the men who left Egypt had been circumcised, but those born in the wilderness had not. The place is called Gilgal, because the LORD has “rolled away the reproach of Egypt.” Israel keeps the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month, eats grain of the land the next day, and the manna stops. Near Jericho, Joshua meets a man with a drawn sword, the captain of the LORD's host, who tells him to take off his shoe, for the ground is holy.

Look at the order. Before a single battle, Israel's fighting men are left unable to fight until they heal (v. 8), a feast is kept within sight of Jericho, and the commander is sent barefoot. The land is entered first through covenant and worship.

5.hermeneutics:
Gods handed swords to kings before battle. In Merneptah's account of his Libyan war, carved at Karnak (c. 1208 BC), the king dreams that a statue of Ptah stands before him and holds out a sword, saying “Take thou (it),” and telling him to banish fear. Ashurbanipal of Assyria (7th century BC) records a seer's dream before his war with Elam in which Ishtar of Arbela appears with quivers and a bow, holding “a sharp sword” unsheathed for battle, and promises to go wherever the king goes. Joshua's visitor also stands before battle with his sword drawn (v. 13), and Joshua asks the obvious question: are you for us? The answer is “Nay.” The captain hands over no sword and takes no side. He comes as commander of the LORD's host, and Joshua falls on his face and takes off his shoe.

Circumcision marked peoples, and Egyptians noticed it. The same Karnak inscription counts the Libyan dead by their uncircumcised members, carried off as trophies, while for the Ekwesh, a sea people “who had no foreskins,” the scribes counted hands instead. Egypt circumcised, and it recorded who did not. Verses 4–7 explain that a whole generation born in the wilderness had grown up without the mark their fathers carried out of Egypt. The rite at Gilgal restores it before any fighting, and it leaves the army in pain for days (v. 8) beside a walled city.

notes: **Rolling:** v. 9 explains the name by a pun: the LORD has “rolled away” (*galal*) the reproach, and *Gilgal* sounds like it.
**Circumcise:** the verb comes 8 times in vv. 2–8, with a long explanation (vv. 4–7) that is unusual in the book.

**Holy ground:** v. 15 repeats the words to Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:5): loose the shoe, for “the place whereon thou standest is holy.” Joshua, magnified like Moses in 4:14, now meets God as Moses did.

Chapter 5 closes the book's first section, the entry into the land (chapters 1–5). Verse 1 looks back to the crossing, and the circumcision, the Passover, and the end of the manna prepare the people; the captain prepares their leader. His message seems to run on into 6:2–5, where the LORD gives the plan for Jericho, so the chapter break may cut one scene in two.
**Backward and forward:** the Passover at Gilgal answers the one kept at Sinai (Numbers 9:5). Gilgal later becomes a shrine the prophets condemn (Hosea 4:15; Amos 4:4).

traditions.text: The Church's footnote to v. 15 points to a revelation naming Far West, Missouri, as a gathering place for the Saints. The Lord calls it a holy and consecrated land, “for the ground upon which thou standest is holy.” The words given to Moses at the bush and to Joshua outside Jericho are applied to a Latter-day Saint city.

Why had the wilderness generation gone uncircumcised (vv. 5–7)? The Talmud offers two answers: the travelers were too weary, or the north wind, needed for healing, never blew in those forty years, either as a punishment after the spies or so the clouds of glory would not scatter. On “the second time” (v. 2), Rabba bar Yitzhak says some who had been circumcised in Abraham's manner needed the rite completed as the law given at Sinai required.

What was “the reproach of Egypt” (v. 9)? Rashi, following Moses ha-Darshan, says the Egyptians had taunted Israel with a star called Ra'ah, a sign of blood, which they claimed would overpower them in the wilderness (Exodus 10:10). The blood they foresaw, he says, was the blood of circumcision, and when it was shed at Gilgal the taunt was rolled away.

Josephus says nothing about the circumcision at Gilgal. He does explain the name: the camp was called Gilgal, which “denotes liberty,” because once across the Jordan the Hebrews counted themselves free of what they had suffered in Egypt and the wilderness. He has the manna fail as they began to reap the Canaanites' ripe grain.

Both explain why the manna stopped. Pseudo-Philo says that after Moses died the manna ceased, because God gave three gifts for the sake of three persons: the well for Miriam, the pillar of cloud for Aaron, and the manna for Moses; when the three died, the gifts were taken away. A baraita in the Talmud gives the same three gifts and merits, which numbers-020 cites for Miriam's well; here the manna's end in v. 12 is tied to Moses' death.

The Talmud asks how Joshua could bow to an unknown figure at night, and answers that a demon does not speak the name of God in vain. The captain, it says, came to rebuke Joshua for neglecting the afternoon offering and, that night, the study of Torah; “now am I come” shows the second fault was the graver. Rashi identifies the captain as the angel Michael, who had offered to go with Moses and been refused (Exodus 33:15).

The Aramaic Targum keeps the scene but changes the visitor's title. When Joshua asks whether he has come to help Israel, he answers that he is an angel sent from before the LORD, and it is this angel who tells Joshua to remove his shoe. The Targum also says the generation of v. 6 died because they did not accept the Memra, the Word, of the LORD.

Justin makes two uses of this chapter. To prove that the one who appeared to the patriarchs was the Son, begotten before all creatures, he quotes vv. 13–15 in full: Joshua worships the captain of the Lord's host. And he reads the “knives of stone” of v. 2 as Christ's words, by which those who entered the holy land with the true Joshua are circumcised in heart from idols of stone.

Lactantius lists v. 2 among prophecies that circumcision of the flesh would give way to circumcision of the heart. He notices that the text says the Lord spoke “unto Jesus,” not to the prophet himself, and takes it as addressed to Christ, the true Jesus. He adds that Moses had renamed Auses as Jesus when he chose him to lead against Amalek.

Describing Paula's pilgrimage, Jerome has her look on the camp of Gilgal and the hill of the foreskins, “suggestive of the mystery of the second circumcision,” and he cites Paul's circumcision of the heart (Romans 2:28–29). The place named in v. 3 had become a stop on the pilgrim road.

Eusebius places Gilgal east of old Jericho toward the Jordan. There, he says, Joshua circumcised the people and kept the Passover, eating wheat for the first time after the manna ceased, and the tent of witness stood. The deserted site, two miles from Jericho, was still held sacred by people of the region, and under “the hill of the foreskins” he notes the stones from the Jordan shown nearby.

6.overview:
Jericho is shut tight against Israel. The LORD tells Joshua the city is already given and lays out a strange plan. For six days the armed men, seven priests blowing rams’ horns, and the ark go once around the walls while the people keep silent; on the seventh day they go around seven times. At the long blast the people shout, the wall falls flat, and Israel goes straight in. Every living thing is destroyed, the metal goes to the LORD’s treasury, and the city is burned. Rahab and her family are brought out alive, and Joshua lays a curse on anyone who rebuilds Jericho.

Watch the exception. The whole city is declared “accursed” to the LORD, devoted and off limits, and the one household spared belongs to a Canaanite harlot who hid Israel’s messengers. In the next chapter the line runs the other way: a man of Judah takes what was devoted and dies with his house.

6.hermeneutics:
The Ugaritic epic of Kirta (13th century BC or earlier) has the god El tell King Kirta how to take the city of Udum. He is to wait outside it for six days without shooting arrows at the city or slinging stones at its walls. On the seventh day the king of Udum, kept awake by the noise of his own animals, sends messengers offering silver, gold and horses for peace. A siege counted in six days with a decisive seventh was a known shape for a war story in Canaan. Joshua 6 uses that shape and changes what the seventh day brings: no envoys come out, and the wall falls.

Around 1700 BC the Anatolian king Anitta took the city of Hattusa, destroyed it, sowed its ground with weeds, and declared that if any king after him resettled it, the Storm-god of heaven should strike him. A curse on rebuilding marked a city as given over to defeat for good. Joshua’s oath in v. 26 belongs to that practice, but sets the price inside the rebuilder’s own family, his firstborn at the foundation and his youngest at the gates.

Jericho is Tell es-Sultan, beside the spring. John Garstang (1930–36) found fallen walls and a burned city and dated its end to about 1400 BC. Kathleen Kenyon (1952–58) showed that his walls were far older and dated the burned city to about 1550 BC, leaving little or nothing for Joshua to take; radiocarbon dates on grain from that burn layer (1995) agree with her. Bryant Wood (1990) restudied her pottery and argued again for about 1400 BC. Recent Italian–Palestinian excavations found a smaller Late Bronze town whose upper levels were later cut away. Most archaeologists follow Kenyon’s date, a minority follow Wood, and the site has not settled the question.

notes: **Sevens:** “seven” comes 11 times and “seventh” 3 times, 14 in all. The verb “compass” comes 7 times (vv. 3, 4, 7, 11, 14, and twice in v. 15).

**Horns and ark:** the Hebrew for the trumpet, *shofar*, comes 14 times, and the ark is named 10 times in vv. 4–13, then not again. The procession is told as worship, and the soldiers do nothing until the shout.
**Silence and shout:** the verb “shout” comes 7 times, three of them in v. 10, where Joshua forbids it until the day he commands it.
**Rahab breaks in:** both the order to destroy (v. 17) and its carrying out (vv. 21–25) stop to make room for her.

Chapter 6 opens the conquest (6:1–12:24) and stands as its own unit, from Jericho “straitly shut up” (v. 1) to Joshua’s fame “noised throughout all the country” (v. 27). It closes the Rahab story of ch. 2: the household gathered under the scarlet line in 2:18–19 is the one brought out in vv. 22–23. Many readers join 5:13–15 to it, since the captain of the LORD’s host appears “by Jericho” just before the LORD speaks in v. 2.
**Forward:** the warning of v. 18 that taking the devoted thing would “trouble” the camp uses the verb that names the valley of Achor in 7:25–26.

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to v. 20, where the wall falls, points to a parable given to the Saints driven from Jackson County. The lord of the vineyard commands his servants to “break down the walls of mine enemies” and throw down their tower. It is a thematic link: the Jericho image is applied to the redemption of Zion.

Before storming the walled town of Caspis, Judas Maccabeus and his men call on the great Lord of the world, the one “who without rams or engines of war did cast down Jericho.” The chapter had become a prayer for besiegers. Judas still assaults the walls himself, and takes the town.

A one-page anthology from Cave 4 lists proof texts for the end of days: the prophet like Moses, Balaam’s star, Levi’s blessing, and, last, Joshua’s curse from v. 26. It then expounds the curse with a passage from the Psalms of Joshua about an accursed man of Belial and two instruments of violence who rebuild a city and shed blood. Scholars read it as an attack on a builder of their own day, often a Hasmonean ruler.

Josephus keeps the six days and seven circuits but adds a pause: after the seventh circuit the army “had stood still a little” before the wall fell, with no instrument of war applied. He says Joshua gave Rahab lands at once and held her in great esteem ever after. On the curse he promises to tell later what came of it.

This retelling names the two spies: Kenaz and Seenamias, sons of Caleb, sent because their father had been a faithful spy before them. Then the whole conquest of Jericho shrinks to one sentence: the people besieged the city and burned it with fire. Rahab, the trumpets and the falling wall are all left out.

This early rabbinic chronicle dates the events: Israel crossed the Jordan on the tenth of Nisan, kept Passover on the fourteenth, and began circling Jericho on the twenty-second. Rabbi Yose adds that the day of battle, the seventh, was a Sabbath. Rashi builds on this: the war was lawful that day because God commanded it, and the city was made “accursed,” holy to the LORD, because the spoil was taken on a holy day.
traditions.cite: Seder Olam Rabbah 11; Rashi on Joshua 6:15, 17

traditions.text: The Aramaic translation fills in v. 1: Jericho was shut with doors of iron and bars of bronze, and no one went out to make war or came in to ask after anyone’s welfare. In v. 5 it renders the wall’s fall as being “swallowed up in its place,” the reading the Talmud also knows (next entry).

The Mishnah says that whoever sees a place where miracles were done for Israel blesses God who did miracles for the fathers there. The Talmud’s list of such places includes the crossings of the Jordan, the hailstones at Beth-horon, and “the wall of Jericho that was swallowed.” The detail comes from v. 5, where the wall falls, literally, “under itself”: it sank where it stood rather than toppling outward.

A baraita widens Joshua’s curse: no one may build Jericho under another name, nor give Jericho’s name to another city. Hiel, the Talmud says, buried all his sons one by one from the firstborn to the youngest and should have read the warning in the first death. Elijah and King Ahab visit his house of mourning, and Ahab scoffs that if Moses’ curse of drought has not come, Joshua’s should not either; Elijah answers with the drought of 1 Kings 17:1.

The great chapter on faith gives Jericho one line: “By faith the walls of Jericho fell down,” after seven days of circling. The faith meant is an army’s willingness to march around a wall for a week with nothing to show for it until the seventh day. Rahab follows in the next verse (see chapter 2).

Origen reads Jericho as the world, which will end not by sword or battering ram but at the sound of a trumpet, as Paul says the last day will come. Only the harlot and her household are spared, and he takes Rahab as a figure of the Church and her scarlet cord as a sign of salvation by Christ’s blood. Since Joshua’s name in Greek is Jesus, Origen speaks of the Lord Jesus taking Jericho.

7.overview:
About three thousand men go up against Ai, run, and lose thirty-six. Joshua and the elders lie on their faces before the ark until evening, and Joshua asks why God brought Israel over the Jordan. The LORD answers that Israel has sinned: someone has taken of the devoted thing. Next morning the lot narrows from tribe to family to household to man and falls on Achan of Judah. He confesses that he saw a fine garment, silver, and a wedge of gold, coveted them, and hid them in the ground under his tent. All Israel stones him, burns what was his, and raises a heap of stones over him in the valley of Achor.

One man takes, and the LORD says “Israel hath sinned” (v. 11). The chapter starts the same way, charging the trespass to “the children of Israel” before it names Achan. The guilt belongs to the whole camp until it is found and removed.

7.hermeneutics:
A Hittite manual for temple staff, the *Instructions for Temple Officials* (14th–13th century BC), forbids officials to keep the gods’ silver and gold for themselves. Anyone who secretly sells or hides temple silver, gold, garments or bronze is to die, and so is the one who receives it. The same text asks whether a god who has been angered takes revenge on the offender alone, and answers that the god strikes his wife, his children, his descendants, his slaves, his cattle and his grain. Achan’s haul is exactly the kind of goods the manual names, and Jericho’s metal had already been set apart for “the treasury of the LORD” (6:19, 24). The sentence on his whole household in v. 24 rests on the same belief, that a man’s house stands or falls with him before his god.

Achan’s first item is “a goodly Babylonish garment,” in Hebrew a mantle of Shinar, the old name for Babylonia (Genesis 11:2). Mesopotamian cloth was a luxury export. In the 19th century BC Assyrian merchants carried donkey-loads of textiles to Kanesh in Anatolia and sold them for silver and gold, and their records describe some of the cloth as “Akkadian,” that is, Babylonian. A Babylonian mantle in a Canaanite town was an imported prize. It sat beside two hundred shekels of silver, roughly two and a quarter kilograms, and a gold bar of fifty shekels, and Achan names it first.

notes: **The devoted thing:** the Hebrew *herem*, “accursed thing,” comes 8 times (twice in v. 1, then vv. 11, 12 twice, 13 twice, 15). In v. 12 Israel itself has become *herem*.
**Taken:** the verb for being “taken” by the lot comes 8 times in vv. 14–18 as the circle shrinks from tribe to man.
**Saw, coveted, took:** Achan’s three verbs in v. 21 are the three of Genesis 3:6, where the woman “saw,” found the tree “to be desired,” and “took.”
**Trouble:** Joshua’s question “Why hast thou troubled us? the LORD shall trouble thee” (v. 25) uses the verb *akar*, which the place name Achor repeats (v. 26).

Chapters 7–8 form one unit. A defeat at Ai is traced to its cause, the cause is removed, Ai is taken (8:1–29), and the unit closes with the altar and the reading of the law on Ebal (8:30–35). Verse 1 picks up the warning of 6:18, and the heap of stones “unto this day” in v. 26 is matched by the heap over the king of Ai in 8:29.
**Forward:** Hosea 2:15 promises to make “the valley of Achor for a door of hope,” and Isaiah 65:10 makes it a resting place for herds.

traditions.text: For the command to sanctify themselves before the lot (v. 13), the footnotes turn from ritual washing to the heart. Helaman describes a sanctification that comes from yielding one’s heart to God, and D&C 88 tells the Saints to sanctify themselves “that your minds become single to God.” These are thematic links supplied by the Church’s cross-references.

Achan’s confession became the model for every condemned man. On the way to execution he is urged to confess, since whoever confesses has a share in the world to come. The proof is v. 25: “the LORD shall trouble thee this day,” which the Mishnah reads as “this day,” and not in the world to come. A man who does not know how to confess is told to say, May my death be atonement for all my sins.

When Joshua asks who sinned, God replies, “Am I an informer?” and sends him to cast lots. Achan objects that a lot proves nothing, since lots cast between Joshua and Eleazar would fall on one of them, and Joshua pleads with him not to discredit the lot by which the land will later be divided. From “Israel hath sinned” (v. 11) Rabbi Abba draws a rule: an Israelite who sins is still Israel, as a myrtle among thorns is still a myrtle.

Rav Huna denies that Achan’s sons and daughters were stoned. All Israel went to the valley too, he argues, and no one thinks they were executed; the family was taken there to watch and be warned. Ravina explains the double penalty of v. 25: what could burn was burned, and what could be stoned was stoned. The same page reads the “about thirty and six men” of v. 5 as one man, Jair son of Manasseh, worth the majority of the seventy-one-member Sanhedrin.

Josephus calls the thief Achar and makes his plunder grander: “a royal garment woven intirely of gold” and a piece of gold weighing two hundred shekels. Achar dug a deep pit in his tent to hide them. After his death, Josephus adds, he was buried at night in a disgraceful manner.

Ananias and Sapphira sell land and secretly keep back part of the price, and both fall dead when Peter exposes them. The verb for “kept back” is the one the Greek Septuagint uses in v. 1 for Israel’s trespass in the devoted thing. In both stories a hidden theft comes just after a triumphant beginning, and the Church’s footnotes to vv. 20–21 point to Acts 5.

Augustine asks how it can be just to punish others for one man’s sin when the law forbids punishing sons for fathers (Deuteronomy 24:16). That law binds human judges, he answers; God may use a death that comes to all anyway to teach a people that they are members of one body. Such a death in this life is not damnation for the innocent in the next.

God said the guilty man would be “burnt with fire” (v. 15), yet Joshua had him stoned. Augustine refuses to think Joshua disobeyed and proposes two readings. Either the stoning was itself the “fire” of a cleansing punishment that spared Achan from eternal loss, or the burning foretold what God himself would do to him after death.

traditions.source: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy
traditions.text: Ambrose makes Achan his example of the love of money, an old vice that nearly cost Israel its victory. He sets Joshua’s two contests side by side: “At the sound of his voice the sun stood still,” but greed did not stop. The man who could hold back the sun could not hold back avarice in his own camp.
traditions.cite: On the Duties of the Clergy 2.26.129–130

traditions.text: Eusebius’ gazetteer places the valley of Achor north of Jericho and says the people nearby still called it by that name. It explains the name as the valley where Achar was stoned, the one who stole what was under the ban. Jerome’s Latin version adds that the prophet Hosea mentions it.

8.overview:
This time the LORD sends all the fighting men and supplies the plan. A force lies hidden west of Ai, between it and Beth-el, while Joshua comes up openly from the north. When the men of Ai come out, Israel pretends to flee as before, and the whole city, Beth-el’s men with it, pours out in pursuit. At Joshua’s signal with his outstretched spear the ambush enters the empty city and sets it on fire, and the men of Ai are caught between the two forces. Ai is burned and left a heap, and its king is hanged and buried under stones at the gate. Then Joshua builds an altar on mount Ebal, writes the law on stones, and reads all of it to the gathered people.

Notice what is allowed this time: the cattle and spoil forbidden at Jericho are Israel’s to keep (vv. 2, 27). What Achan stole is handed out freely one battle later.

8.hermeneutics:
At Kadesh on the Orontes in 1274 BC the Hittite king Muwatalli II hid his army “behind the old city of Kadesh,” while two Shasu tribesmen told Ramesses II that the Hittites were far away to the north. Ramesses marched up, and Hittite chariots came out from behind the city and broke one of his divisions on the move. Egypt’s most celebrated battle of the age turned on a force hidden behind a city. Joshua 8 uses it with one difference. The bait is Ai’s own memory of winning, as Joshua predicts the defenders will say, “They flee before us, as at the first” (v. 6).

The name Ai means “the ruin,” and v. 28 says Joshua made it a *tel*, a ruin mound, forever. The usual identification is et-Tell, Arabic for “the mound,” east of Beitin (Bethel). Judith Marquet-Krause (1933–35) and Joseph Callaway (1960s–70s) found a large walled Early Bronze city destroyed about 2400 BC, no settlement in the Middle or Late Bronze Ages, and a small Iron Age village. At any date proposed for Joshua there was no city there to take. Martin Noth read the story as an explanation of a famous ruin; W. F. Albright thought a battle for nearby Bethel had been moved to it. Others say et-Tell is the wrong site: Bryant Wood’s excavations at nearby Khirbet el-Maqatir found a small fortress burned in the late 15th century BC, though most scholars have not accepted that identification. There is no consensus.

notes: **Ambush:** the Hebrew verb and noun for lying in wait come 7 times (vv. 2, 4, 7, 12, 14, 19, 21), and Ai is named 23 times in vv. 1–29.

**The spear:** “stretch out” comes 4 times (twice in v. 18, then vv. 19, 26). Joshua “drew not his hand back” until the end (v. 26), as Moses held up his hands until Amalek was beaten (Exodus 17:11–12).
**Two numbers:** the ambush is 30,000 in v. 3 and 5,000 in v. 12, and readers have long asked whether these are one force or two.
**All the words:** the closing scene stresses completeness: “all the words of the law” (v. 34), not a word left unread (v. 35).

Verses 1–29 reverse 7:2–5 point by point: all the people go up instead of a few (v. 1; 7:3), the men of Ai chase Israel again, and a heap of stones over the king (v. 29) answers the one over Achan (7:26). Verses 30–35 close the unit by carrying out Deuteronomy 27, though ancient witnesses place them at different points in the story.
**Forward:** Judges 20:29–48 tells the ambush of Gibeah in the same pattern, down to the defenders’ boast “as at the first” (Judges 20:32).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to “liers in wait” (v. 13) points to Captain Moroni’s ambushes. At Mulek, Moroni decoys the Lamanites out of their stronghold: Teancum’s small band shows itself and retreats, the Lamanites pursue, and Moroni’s men enter the city and take it. Alma 43:30–43 and 58:15–21 describe other hidden forces in the same war.

The oldest surviving copy of Joshua places the reading of the law (vv. 34–35, in a longer form) right after the crossing of the Jordan and before the circumcision of 5:2. In that order the first altar in the land stands at Gilgal, as the twelve stones do, before any battle. Many scholars take this as evidence that the passage moved around as the book was copied.

The Greek translation puts vv. 30–35 after 9:1–2, once the kings of Canaan have gathered against Israel and just before the Gibeonites arrive. Its version of v. 35 reads the law to “the men, and the women, and the children,” and to the strangers who joined Israel. So three ancient witnesses give three positions for one ceremony.

Josephus tells the ambush simply: Joshua laid it by night and drew the defenders a great way from the city by making them believe he had retreated. He holds the Ebal ceremony back until the fifth year, after the tabernacle is set up at Shiloh. Then the people stand half on Gerizim and half on Ebal, “on which mountain the altar was,” and return to Shiloh.

Pseudo-Philo moves the altar still later, to the end of Joshua’s life after the land is divided. Joshua goes down from Gilgal, builds an altar of great stones untouched by iron, whitens stones on Ebal and writes the law on them, then reads it to all the people. The ark is carried out of the tabernacle with timbrels, harps and dancing, and Israel sings that God has kept his word to the fathers.

The rabbis put the ceremony on the very day Israel crossed the Jordan; the Talmud’s account of that crowded day is told under chapter 4. Seder Olam lists it before the circumcision of 5:2 and the Passover, and Rashi therefore says v. 30 is out of chronological order. On “half of them over against mount Gerizim” (v. 33), Rav Kahana says the tribes stood divided as their names were divided on the two shoulder stones of the high priest’s ephod.
traditions.cite: Seder Olam Rabbah 11; Rashi on Joshua 8:30; b. Sotah 36a

traditions.text: Rashi meets the two numbers for the ambush (vv. 3, 12) by making them two parties. The five thousand of v. 12 were a second band placed nearer the city, one ambush beyond the other. His annotators suggest its task was to strike Ai’s army from behind while it chased Israel.

Origen reads the altar of unhewn stones (v. 31) as the apostles, untouched by iron and made one altar by their unity of mind and heart. Believers who give themselves to prayer day and night, he says, become living stones in the altar Jesus is building. The homily survives in Rufinus’ Latin.

God’s order to “lay thee an ambush” (v. 2) shows Augustine that stratagems are not forbidden in a just war. Once a war is just, he says, it makes no difference to justice whether it is won in open battle or by ambush. Here he gives the definition later writers repeated, that just wars avenge injuries, and adds that a war God commands is just, with leader and people its executors more than its authors.

In the next question Augustine turns to Joshua’s words in vv. 5–6, “we will flee before them,” spoken to deceive. He asks whether every intent to deceive is a lie and, if so, whether one may lie to an enemy who deserves to be deceived. If not even then, he says, some hidden meaning must excuse the stratagem, and he leaves the question there.

Eusebius places Aggai, his spelling of Ai, west of Bethel and not far from it, though 7:2 puts Ai on Bethel’s east side. The Latin edition, with Jerome’s additions, says only ruins of the place were shown, and notes that Hebrew has no G: the name begins with the letter *ayin*. Its fourth-century reader knew Ai, as the name says, as a ruin.

9.overview:
The kings west of the Jordan band together against Israel, but the people of Gibeon try a trick instead. Envoys arrive at the camp in Gilgal in patched sandals and worn-out clothes, with cracked wineskins and dry, crumbling bread, saying they come from a very far country because of the fame of Israel’s God. The men of Israel take some of their food without asking counsel of the LORD, and Joshua and the princes swear a treaty to let them live. Three days later Israel learns they are neighbors, from four towns close by. The princes refuse to break their oath, and Joshua makes the Gibeonites woodcutters and water carriers for the congregation and the altar.

The lie is aimed at the law. Deuteronomy 20 lets Israel make peace with cities “very far off from thee” (20:15) but not with the nations of the land, the Hivites among them (20:17). The worn-out gear is forged proof of distance.

9.hermeneutics:
Most letters from Canaan in the Amarna archive (14th century BC) were written to Pharaoh by kings of city-states, but a few come from towns without one. A letter from Irqata in Lebanon is sent by the city and its elders, and one from Tunip in Syria by its citizens, both pledging loyalty to Egypt. Gibeon fits that pattern. Its envoys speak for “our elders and all the inhabitants of our country” (v. 11) and no king is named, though 10:2 calls Gibeon “a great city, as one of the royal cities.” Their repeated “We are thy servants” (vv. 8, 11) is the language a vassal used in those letters when asking a stronger power for protection.

Gibeon is el-Jib, north-west of Jerusalem. James Pritchard’s excavations (1956–62) settled the identification when jar handles inscribed with the name *gb‘n*, Gibeon, turned up, most of them in a great rock-cut pool. They belong to a wine industry of the 8th–7th centuries BC, and Gibeon also appears in the list of towns Pharaoh Shoshenq I claimed on his campaign in the late 10th century BC. No Late Bronze Age town has been found there, only a few tombs with imported Cypriot pottery. Pritchard suggested the town of Joshua’s day lay in an unexcavated part of the mound; others take the gap to mean the story reflects a later Gibeon. As at Jericho and Ai, the question is open.

notes: **Props:** the word “old” comes 4 times in vv. 4–5, on sacks, wineskins, shoes and garments, and v. 13 walks the reader back through the same items.
**Far and near:** “far” comes 3 times (vv. 6, 9, 22), while the fear that they “dwell among us” comes in vv. 7, 16 and 22.
**The oath:** “league” (*berit*) comes 5 times (vv. 6, 7, 11, 15, 16) and “sware” 4 times (vv. 15, 18, 19, 20). Once sworn, the oath controls the rest of the chapter.
**Hewers and drawers:** the phrase comes 3 times (vv. 21, 23, 27), serving first the congregation, then “the house of my God,” then both congregation and altar.

Chapters 9–10 form one unit. The coalition gathered in vv. 1–2 does not move until Gibeon’s treaty gives it a target, and the five kings’ attack on Gibeon (10:1–5) brings Joshua south. The Gibeonites’ “we have heard” of Egypt, Sihon and Og (vv. 9–10) echoes Rahab’s speech (2:10), another Canaanite household that lives among Israel by an oath.

**Backward and forward:** Deuteronomy 29:11 already counts the hewer of wood and the drawer of water within the covenant assembly. Centuries later “the men of Gibeon” help rebuild Jerusalem’s wall (Nehemiah 3:7).

traditions.text: The Church’s footnote to v. 14, where Israel did not ask the LORD before swearing, points to two counsels in the Book of Mormon. Jacob warns against counseling the Lord and urges his people to “take counsel from his hand,” and Alma tells his son Helaman to counsel with the Lord in all his doings. The footnote also cites Numbers 27:21, the rule that Joshua was to ask counsel through Eleazar and the Urim.

traditions.date: 1st century BC and 1st century AD (Book of Mormon)
traditions.text: For the “league” of v. 7 the footnotes point to Nephite covenants of peace with former enemies. Lamanites who laid down their weapons and covenanted peace with Moroni were let go into the wilderness, and robbers who covenanted to keep the peace were later given lands to live on. As with Gibeon, a sworn promise turns an enemy into a protected neighbor.

Josephus has Eleazar the high priest and the senate swear the oath along with Joshua, promising to treat the Gibeonites as friends and associates. When Joshua learns they are Canaanites he reproaches them for the cheat, but the oath cannot be broken, so they are made public servants. Josephus then moves straight to Joshua rescuing them from the five kings, as if the oath had made Gibeon Israel’s ally as well as its servant.

Verse 4 says the Gibeonites “also” worked wilily, and Rashi asks whom they copied. His answer reaches back to Genesis 34: Jacob’s sons tricked Hamor the Hivite at Shechem, and the Gibeonites, Hivites themselves (v. 7), answered trickery with trickery. He derives the rare verb for posing as envoys from the Hebrew word for messenger, and says the worn sacks were meant to look like gear from a distant land.

In a debate over whether a public vow can be annulled, one side cites v. 18: Israel did not strike the Gibeonites because the princes had sworn. The Sages answer that the oath never took effect, since it rested on the false claim “We be come from a far country.” Israel spared them anyway for the sanctity of God’s name: killing them after a public oath, even an empty one, would have desecrated it.

Reading 2 Samuel 21, the Talmud has David try to appease the Gibeonites for Saul’s killings. When they demand seven of Saul’s sons, he names three marks of Israel, mercy, modesty and kindness, and bars the Gibeonites from marrying into Israel. Joshua’s sentence in v. 27, the Talmud adds, held only while the altar stood, since it was “for the altar of the LORD,” while David’s decree held for all time.

traditions.source: Ambrose, On the Duties of the Clergy
traditions.text: Ambrose uses this chapter to show that Scripture condemned fraud in agreements long before the Roman lawyers did. He excuses Joshua’s failure to see through the Gibeonites, since good men believe others as truthful as themselves. Joshua kept the peace sworn by oath rather than break his own pledge in punishing their treachery, and the mild but lasting penalty of hereditary service was the price of their cunning. In Book 1 he sets this restraint toward a people who tried Israel “with guile rather than with war” beside Moses’ severity toward Midian.
traditions.cite: On the Duties of the Clergy 3.10.66–69; 1.29.139

traditions.text: Augustine asks why Israel kept an oath obtained by a lie, and answers that God approved: he was not angry with the oath or with the mercy shown, and later avenged the Gibeonites on Saul’s house as if they were his own people. The Gibeonites, he adds, truly feared God and his people for all their pretense. An oath that leans toward mercy should be kept, while David rightly broke his oath to kill Nabal (1 Samuel 25).

In the question before, Augustine notes that some Greek and Latin copies of v. 4 have the Gibeonites carry their old sacks on their shoulders. Others, more credible, have them on their asses, and he blames the near-identical Greek words *ōmois* and *onois*. Envoys from a distant nation, carrying wineskins as well as sacks, would have used pack animals.

Eusebius remembers Gibeon as once a great royal city of the Hivites, from which came the Gibeonites who made supplication to Joshua. In his day a village of the same name stood four miles west of Bethel near Ramah. He also lists Chephirah as a village belonging to Gibeon and Beeroth at the foot of Gibeon’s hill, both named in v. 17.

10.overview:
Adoni-zedek of Jerusalem hears that Gibeon has made peace with Israel and leads five Amorite kings against it. Gibeon sends to Gilgal for help. Joshua marches all night, falls on the coalition, and chases it down the pass of Beth-horon while the LORD throws great stones from heaven. Joshua speaks to the sun and moon, and the day holds until the victory is won. The five kings hide in a cave at Makkedah; Joshua's captains put their feet on the kings' necks, and the kings are killed and hanged until evening. Joshua then takes the southern towns one after another and returns to Gilgal.

The chapter quotes its most famous lines. The words to the sun and moon (vv. 12–13) are a piece of poetry, and the narrator points to where he found them: “Is not this written in the book of Jasher?” He expects his readers to know an older written collection, now lost.

10.hermeneutics:
Mesopotamian scribes watched the sun and moon for omens, and the middle of the month mattered most. In the omen series *Enuma Anu Enlil*, the full moon and the sun seen together on opposite horizons on the fourteenth day was a good sign for the king; seen together on the wrong day, texts warn, a powerful enemy would raise his weapons against the land. The verbs for this were “stand” and “wait.” John Walton (1994), following a suggestion of John Holladay (1968), argued that vv. 12–13 use that vocabulary. With the sun over Gibeon in the east and the moon over Ajalon in the west it is morning, and Joshua asks for a sign that would spell defeat for the Amorites. Others read the verses as a lengthened day, as Josephus did, or as an eclipse. There is no consensus, but the omen reading explains why the moon is in the poem at all.

Conquest reports across the ancient Near East were written in stock phrases. Egyptian, Hittite and Assyrian annals claim that a king took “all the land” and left no survivors, and K. Lawson Younger (1990) showed how closely Joshua 9–12 follows that style. Verses 28–39 run through six towns in nearly the same words: Joshua passes on, fights, takes the town, strikes it with the sword, and leaves none remaining, as he had done to the last. Read the way such annals were read, the refrain claims a decisive campaign more than it counts the dead. The book itself points that way: Hebron and Debir, emptied here (vv. 36–39), must be taken again by Caleb and Othniel (15:13–17). Younger's is one scholarly reading; others take the totals more literally.

notes: **Two endings:** v. 15 and v. 43 use the same words, though the story goes on at Makkedah in between. The Septuagint lacks both verses, and it also lacks the question about the book of Jasher.

**The refrain:** “the edge of the sword” comes six times in vv. 28–39, and the Hebrew word for a survivor (*sarid*), “none remaining,” comes seven times in the chapter (vv. 20, 28, 30, 33, 37, 39, 40). Each town is measured against one already taken.
**Fought:** the verb “fight” runs nine times through the chapter. Twice the subject is the LORD, who “fought for Israel” (vv. 14, 42).

Chapters 9–10 belong together: the Gibeonite treaty is why the southern kings attack (vv. 1, 4). The campaign ends where it began, at the camp at Gilgal (v. 43), and 11:1 opens the northern war the same way, with a king who “had heard.” Jasher itself is lost; the “Book of Jasher” printed in English in 1840 translates a Hebrew retelling first printed in Venice in 1625, not the book quoted here.

**Echoes:** Isaiah recalls the LORD's anger “as in the valley of Gibeon” (Isaiah 28:21), and Habakkuk's hymn has sun and moon standing still “in their habitation” (Habakkuk 3:11). Jasher is quoted again for David's lament over Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:18).

traditions.text: In an aside on the power of God's word, Mormon writes that if the Lord commands the earth to go back so as to lengthen the day for many hours, it is done. Seen from the ground, he explains, the sun only appears to stand still, “for surely it is the earth that moveth and not the sun.” He names no battle, but the lengthened day and the standing sun are the language of vv. 12–14.

A thematic link. After mob violence against the Saints in Missouri, the Lord describes the law of war he gave to “mine ancients”: they were to go to battle only at his command, and then “I, the Lord, would fight their battles.” The promise runs until they had avenged themselves on all their enemies, close to the wording of v. 13 and the refrain that the LORD fought for Israel (vv. 14, 42).

Ben Sira's praise of Israel's famous men gives this battle its own lines: did not the sun go back by his means, and was not “one day as long as two”? He keeps the chapter's order, with Joshua calling on the Most High and hailstones striking the nations at the descent of Beth-horon. His “go back” is the same picture Mormon uses in Helaman 12.

Josephus adds thunder and thunderbolts to the hail and gives the long day a practical purpose: it kept night from cutting short the Hebrews' pursuit. In place of the book of Jasher he says the lengthened day is recorded “in the Books laid up in the temple.” He counts the allied kings as four besides the king of Jerusalem.

The Talmud asks what the book of Jasher (“the upright”) is. Rabbi Yohanan says it is Genesis, the book of the upright patriarchs, where Jacob foretold that Ephraim's seed would fill the nations (Genesis 48:19); that came true when the sun stood still for Joshua the Ephraimite, and Rashi follows this reading. Other sages name Deuteronomy or Judges, and they differ over how long the sun stood: twenty-four, thirty-six or forty-eight hours.
traditions.cite: b. Avodah Zarah 25a; Rashi on Joshua 10:13

traditions.text: Among places where a passerby blesses God for a miracle, the Talmud lists the stones of Elgavish. They were hail that stopped in midair when Moses prayed in Egypt (Exodus 9:33) and fell at last on the Amorites at Beth-horon. The name is read as “because of a man”: held back for one man, Moses, and let fall for another, Joshua.

Rashi takes “then spake Joshua” as a song of praise and reads the command *dom*, “stand still,” as “be silent.” The sun sings God's praise as it moves, so Joshua silenced it, and while it was silent it stood. As a plainer sense he gives “wait,” as in 1 Samuel 14:9.

Justin reminds his Jewish partner in debate that Israel saw the sun stand still at the order of a man named Jesus, the Greek form of Joshua, and “not go down for thirty-six hours.” His figure is the same as Rabbi Elazar's thirty-six hours in the Talmud (above). For Justin the name was the point: the power at work belonged to the name Jesus.

Origen reads the chapter as a picture of the soul's war. The five kings who hide in the cave are the five bodily senses, which must be brought out of the dark and conquered, and the order to set feet on their necks becomes a command to the believer. His homilies on Joshua survive only in Rufinus' Latin.

Answering skeptics who trusted fixed laws of nature, Augustine cites Varro's report that the planet Venus once changed its color, size and course. Scripture records more, he says: the sun stood still when Joshua asked it of God until the battle was won, and it went back for Hezekiah. Pagans who granted such wonders, he adds, put them down to magic.

Eusebius places the battle on the map of Roman Palestine. Azekah, where Joshua pursued the five kings, is still a village between Eleutheropolis and Jerusalem, and Makkedah lies eight miles east of Eleutheropolis. The valley of Ajalon, “where the moon stood,” he puts near a village of that name three miles east of Bethel; Jerome's Latin version adds that the Hebrews placed it near Nicopolis.

11.overview:
News of the southern victories reaches Jabin, king of Hazor, and he calls up the kings of the north. They camp at the waters of Merom with a host “as the sand that is upon the sea shore” and many horses and chariots. The LORD tells Joshua not to fear and orders him to hamstring the horses and burn the chariots. Joshua strikes suddenly, chases the coalition as far as Sidon, then turns back and burns Hazor, the only city of the north he burns. A summary sweeps the whole land from Mount Halak to Baal-gad, the Anakim are cut off except in three Philistine towns, and “the land rested from war.”

The chapter claims “the whole land” (v. 23) and admits its limits in the same breath. The war took “a long time” (v. 18), and Anakim survive in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod (v. 22). Gath is where Goliath will come from (1 Samuel 17:4).

11.hermeneutics:
Hazor was the largest city in Canaan. Below its upper mound of about 30 acres spread a lower city of some 175 more, far beyond any hill-country town. In the 18th century BC the royal archive of Mari on the Euphrates recorded tin sent to Ibni-Addu, king of Hazor, and Hazor is one of only two Canaanite towns its letters name. Scholars generally take Jabin (*Yabin*) as a short form of the same West Semitic name. In the 14th century the king of Tyre warned Pharaoh that the king of Hazor had gone over to the Habiru (Amarna letter EA 148). Against that background v. 10 reads as plain fact: Hazor “beforetime was the head of all those kingdoms,” the one king able to call up the whole north.

Excavations by Yigael Yadin in the 1950s and by Amnon Ben-Tor since 1990 found that the last Canaanite city ended in a fierce fire, usually dated to the 13th century BC. Ash lay three feet deep in places. In the palace, oil jars and timber drove the heat high enough to turn mudbrick to glass, and statues of gods and kings, Egyptian ones among them, had their heads and hands cut off. Ben-Tor argues that neither Egypt nor a Canaanite rival is likely to have done this and credits early Israel. Sharon Zuckerman saw internal conflict behind it, and Israel Finkelstein points to the wider collapse at the end of the Late Bronze Age. There is no consensus on who burned Hazor.
