notes: **Moses:** his name comes six times (vv. 12, 15 three times, 20, 23), and “commanded” five times in vv. 12–20. The account of the war ends by measuring Joshua against Moses: “he left nothing undone” (v. 15).

**Burning:** the order to burn the chariots (v. 6) is carried out word for word (v. 9), and Hazor alone of the cities is burned (vv. 11, 13). The cities that “stood still” on their mounds (v. 13) use the verb said of the sun in 10:13.
**Breath:** both reports of the slaughter end on the same word, none left “to breathe” (vv. 11, 14).

Chapters 11–12 close the war. Chapter 11 ends the campaigns with a summary of the whole land (vv. 16–23), and ch. 12 turns that summary into a roster of kings. The words “the land rested from war” (v. 23) return at 14:15, after Caleb receives Hebron, and frame the lists between.
**Forward:** Hazor rises again. Deborah and Barak fight “Jabin king of Canaan, that reigned in Hazor” (Judges 4:2), and Solomon later builds it with Megiddo and Gezer (1 Kings 9:15).

traditions.text: Josephus gives the northern host numbers: 300,000 armed footmen, 10,000 horsemen and 20,000 chariots, camped at Beroth near Kedesh in upper Galilee. He says the Israelites were struck with terror until God rebuked their fear, and that Joshua reached the enemy after five days' march. When there were no men left to kill, he slew the horses and burned the chariots. His later Jabin of Judges 4 commands the same 300,000 foot and 10,000 horse.

The midrash counts three times the nations gathered to make war on Jacob's children and God would not let them pursue: after Shechem (Genesis 35:5), in Jonathan's day (1 Samuel 14:15), and in Joshua's day, when they gathered at Hazor (vv. 1–5). That gathering, one view holds, is why Hazor alone was burned. Rabbi Elazar disagrees: Joshua burned it because of a command God gave Moses and Moses passed on, the reading Rashi follows (next entry).

Why was Hazor alone burned (v. 13), when the Torah gives no such order? Rashi takes Rabbi Elazar's answer: Moses received the command by tradition and passed it to Joshua, who carried it out. The other cities kept their walls, unlike Jericho and Ai, which were left as heaps.

Rashi reads “Joshua made war a long time” (v. 18) as a rebuke. Joshua knew he would divide the land and then die, so he drew out the conquest to lengthen his days. For this, the midrash says, he died at 110 instead of reaching Moses' 120. The midrash ties the delay to Moses' charge that Joshua would divide the land among the tribes (Deuteronomy 31:7).

Misrephoth-maim (v. 8) means “burnings of water.” Rashi reports the Aramaic Targum's explanation: the place had trenches where sea water was let in and burned away by the sun, leaving salt. The name became a coastal saltworks known to the Targum's readers, and the pursuit of v. 8 ends at a working landmark on the Phoenician shore.

Maimonides reads vv. 19–20 as proof that peace was offered to every Canaanite city before war. If only Gibeon made peace, he reasons, the others must have been offered terms and refused; the command to leave none alive applied only to those who would not accept. Joshua, he adds, sent the Canaanites word before entering the land: whoever wishes to flee may flee, whoever wishes peace may make peace, whoever wishes war may fight.

In his laws of repentance Maimonides sets the hardening of v. 20 beside Pharaoh and Sihon. A person who sins greatly and by choice may be judged by having repentance withheld, so that he dies in the wickedness he began himself. The Canaanites, he says, were held back from repenting because of their abominable acts, and so came out to fight; God did not decree those acts, they chose them.

Origen takes Jabin's name to mean “prudence” and Hazor to mean “court,” and makes Jabin the devil, whose court is the whole earth. The horses Joshua hamstrings are the bodily passions, lust and pride among them, cut down by fasting and vigils. His Latin translator Rufinus preserved these homilies.

On v. 23 Origen argues that “the land rested from wars” could not be said truly of Joshua's own day. That rest belongs to Christ, he says, and comes to a believer when the wars inside him cease. Hebrews makes a similar argument: if Joshua had given Israel rest, God would not have spoken later of another day (Hebrews 4:8).

In his questions on the books of Moses and Joshua, Augustine reads v. 20 alongside Pharaoh: the Canaanites' hearts were made firm by the Lord, so that they came out to fight. Joshua could not otherwise have destroyed them so quickly, and Israel's own mercy was limited by God's command. On v. 14 he warns readers not to call the slaughter cruelty, since God commanded it and knows what each deserves.

Eusebius lists Hazor as the city of King Jabin that Joshua burned because it was “chief of all the kingdoms.” He knows of another village called Asor in his day, east of Ascalon, and of Madon as the city where Jobab ruled. Jerome's Latin adds that Mount Hermon stands near Paneas and sends snow to Tyre in summer.

12.overview:
The chapter is a roster of defeated kings. First come the two kings Moses defeated east of the Jordan: Sihon of Heshbon, who ruled from the Arnon to the Jabbok, and Og of Bashan, “of the remnant of the giants.” Their land went to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh. Then come the kings Joshua defeated west of the river, from Baal-gad under Lebanon to Mount Halak toward Seir, listed two to a verse: “The king of Jericho, one,” and so on to Tirzah, “all the kings thirty and one.”

The list names more than the story told. Jericho, Ai and the kings of chs. 10–11 are here, but so are kings of Geder, Adullam, Tappuah, Hepher, Aphek, Lasharon, Taanach, Megiddo, Dor and Tirzah, whose defeats are never narrated. Some of those towns are still Canaanite in Judges 1:27.

12.hermeneutics:
In the 14th century BC Canaan was a patchwork of small city-states, each with its own ruler under Egyptian oversight. The Amarna letters, clay tablets these rulers sent to Pharaoh, come from or name the rulers of many towns on this list: Abdi-Heba of Jerusalem, Biridiya of Megiddo, three successive rulers of Gezer, Zimredda and Shipti-Ba'lu of Lachish, the king of Hazor, Indaruta of Achshaph, and Shamu-Adda of Shimron. They accuse one another, form alliances and break them. Thirty-one kings in a land the size of a small modern state is not an inflated number; that is how the country was ruled, each town with its fields and villages under one man. When the list counts each king as “one,” it counts small kingdoms.

Egyptian kings recorded their campaigns in Canaan as lists of conquered towns carved on temple walls. Thutmose III's list at Karnak (15th century BC) names more than a hundred places, and Shoshenq I, the Shishak of 1 Kings 14:25, carved another there about 925 BC with Taanach, Megiddo, Tirzah, Arad, Aijalon and Gibeon among its names. Such lists set out the reach of a victory without telling its story, and their order is not the order of the march. Joshua 12 does the same work for Israel. It gathers the results of chs. 6–11, adds towns whose capture was never narrated, and stands as a monument to the war before the land is divided.

notes: **The count:** the Hebrew word for “one” follows each of the 31 kings, and the total in v. 24 adds a thirty-second (“thirty and one”). The Septuagint's list differs in names and pairings and ends “all these kings twenty-nine.”

**Order:** the western list runs roughly from south to north. It opens with the cities of the story in order (Jericho, Ai, then the southern coalition of ch. 10) and closes with the north of ch. 11 and towns beyond it.
**Two leaders:** each panel names its leader as the one who smote the kings and gave their land (vv. 6–7), so the list sets Joshua's wars beside Moses'.

Chapter 12 closes the first half of the book. After the summary of 11:16–23 it gathers every victory, Moses' and Joshua's, before ch. 13 turns from conquest to division. Its east-then-west order is the order of the allotment that follows: the eastern tribes in ch. 13, the western ones from ch. 14.
**Echo:** Psalm 135 praises the God who “slew mighty kings,” naming Sihon, Og “and all the kingdoms of Canaan,” and gave their land as a heritage to Israel (Psalm 135:10–12).

traditions.text: Josephus has Joshua tell the assembly at Shiloh that thirty-one kings who ventured to fight had been overcome, and every army that trusted its own power destroyed. The remaining cities, he warns, must be taken over time by long sieges because of their strong walls. With that he sends the eastern tribes home with thanks and chooses ten men, with geometricians, to survey the land. His count of the kings is the Hebrew one, not the Septuagint's twenty-nine.

Rabbi Judah asks whether all thirty-one kings were really natives of the land of Israel. His answer comes from his own world: just as every king and governor of his day felt he had achieved nothing until he owned a palace or villa in Rome, so foreign kings had to own an estate in the land of Israel. Elsewhere the Sifre says the kings Joshua subdued ruled dominions reaching to the ends of the earth.

The Talmud describes how scribes lay out the songs of scripture: a short phrase over a blank space, like half bricks set over whole ones in a wall. Two lists are written differently, phrase over phrase and space over space: the ten sons of Haman (Esther 9) and the kings of Canaan of this chapter. A wall built that way cannot stand, and so, the rabbis say, those kings would never rise from their fall.

When God tells Moses “now shalt thou see what I will do to Pharaoh” (Exodus 6:1), the midrash hears a limit: Moses would see the war with Pharaoh but not the wars with the thirty-one kings, which his disciple Joshua would fight. Rashi has Moses plead for exactly that in Deuteronomy 3:24: you have shown me Sihon and Og, show me also the war with the thirty-one kings. The two panels of this chapter mark the line Moses could not cross.

When Moses pleads for Israel after the spies' report, he fears the nations will say the LORD was unable to bring them in (Numbers 14:16). Rashi spells out the taunt: one king, Pharaoh, is not like thirty-one kings who live in Canaan. The number of the list became shorthand for the strength of the land and for the size of what God did when Israel finally entered it.

Rashi reads the Song of Songs as Israel's history with God. When the bride says she found the one she loved soon after she passed the watchmen (Song of Songs 3:4), he hears Israel after Moses and Aaron died: God was with them in Joshua's days to conquer the thirty-one kings. She held him and would not let go until she brought him to the tabernacle at Shiloh (Joshua 18:1).

The midrash counts Joshua's good fortune in the terms of this list: he slew thirty-one kings, gave Israel the land and divided it, and the people pledged to obey him, an honor Moses never had. Yet he did not stay in his happiness, it says, for he died without sons. It reads Psalm 75:4, “Deal not foolishly,” as a warning to the merrymakers.

Surveying the history from Moses to the kings, Augustine pairs the two leaders whose victories this chapter lists. Under Moses and Joshua, he says, Israel's wars went wonderfully well, and God made clear that the victories came less from the merit of the Hebrews than from the sins of the nations they subdued. That Joshua and not Moses led the people into the land, with his name changed to Jesus, he takes as a figure of Christ.

Eusebius gives many towns on the list an entry of their own, nearly always noting that Joshua killed its king. Lachish was still a village seven miles south of Eleutheropolis. Gezer, a village called Gazara four miles north of Nicopolis, prompts the comment that the tribe of Ephraim never drove out its people, as Joshua 16:10 says.

In the north, Eusebius places Taanach, whose king Joshua besieged and killed, four miles from Legio, the Roman legionary camp beside Megiddo. Jokneam is simply “City of Carmel,” and Tirzah, last on the list, is a town Joshua “took along with its king.” For Christian readers in Roman Palestine, the roster could still be walked.

13.overview:
Joshua is old, and the LORD tells him that very much land remains: the Philistine coast with its five lords, the Geshurites, the coast toward Sidon, the land of the Giblites, and Lebanon up to the entering of Hamath. God will drive those peoples out himself; Joshua is to divide the land by lot now. The chapter then looks back across the Jordan and draws the borders of what Moses gave: Reuben from the Arnon to Heshbon, Gad in Gilead up to the Sea of Chinnereth, and half of Manasseh in Bashan. In passing it notes that Israel killed Balaam, and twice it says that Levi received no land (vv. 14, 33).

Joshua is told to divide land Israel does not hold (vv. 6–7). The division of the land opens with a list of what was not conquered, and v. 13 adds that the Geshurites and Maachathites still live among Israel “until this day.”

13.hermeneutics:
The “five lords of the Philistines” (v. 3) ruled a league of five coastal cities: Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath and Ekron. Their title, *seren*, is not a Semitic word. Many scholars link it to Greek *tyrannos*, itself probably borrowed from Anatolia, and see in it the background of a people who came from the Aegean world. In 1996 excavators at Tel Miqne found a 7th-century BC inscription in which Achish son of Padi, “ruler of Ekron,” dedicates a temple to his goddess, which settled the site as Ekron. The land that remains is no empty frontier. It is a confederation with its own rulers and institutions, and it stays outside Israel's grasp through Judges and Samuel (Judges 3:3).

The Moabite king Mesha's victory stone (about 840 BC) names a run of the towns this chapter gives to Reuben: Aroer by the Arnon, Medeba, Dibon, Baal-meon, Kiriathaim and Jahaz (vv. 16–19). Mesha says the men of Gad had lived in the land of Ataroth from of old, but he never mentions Reuben. Many scholars take the silence to mean that Reuben had faded as a tribe by the 9th century, its tableland held by Gad or lost to Moab; Genesis 49:4 and Deuteronomy 33:6 already speak of Reuben as weak. Read with Mesha, vv. 15–23 map a claim on the most contested ground in Transjordan, a border tribe's land between Israel and Moab, which Reuben could not hold for long.

notes: **Inheritance:** the Hebrew *nachalah* comes nine times, twice in each of the Levi verses (vv. 14, 33). The frame moves from the LORD's offerings to the LORD himself.
**Moses gave:** Moses is named nine times. Each tribal section opens with “Moses gave” (vv. 15, 24, 29), and Reuben's and Gad's close with “This is the inheritance of …” (vv. 23, 28).
**Remaining:** the verb for what “remains” opens the prologue twice (vv. 1–2) and returns for Og, of the “remnant” of the giants (v. 12).

Chapter 13 opens the book's second half, the division of the land (chs. 13–21), with a fresh start: Joshua “was old and stricken in years” (v. 1), words that return at 23:1 to open his farewell. It deals first with the land east of the Jordan, already granted by Moses (Numbers 32), before the western lots begin at 14:1.
**Backward:** Balaam's death (v. 22) repeats Numbers 31:8, and the frame on Levi echoes Numbers 18:20 and Deuteronomy 18:1–2.

traditions.text: Josephus explains why so much land remained: Joshua, now old, saw that the Canaanite cities were hard to take, set on strong sites and walled, because the Canaanites had spent the whole time since Israel left Egypt fortifying them. He adds that the parts about Sidon and the lands of the Arkites, Amathites and Aradians were not yet properly allotted, the same northern stretch v. 6 leaves to God; where Joshua 13 says the LORD will drive those peoples out, Josephus gives a soldier's reason the war had stalled. Later, hindered by age, Joshua charges each tribe to leave no Canaanites in the land that fell to it by lot.

The midrash names three men “crowned with old age and length of days,” each described in scripture as old and advanced in years: Abraham (Genesis 24:1), Joshua (v. 1) and David (1 Kings 1:1). Each began a line. Abraham began the patriarchs, David the kings of Judah, and Joshua, read into Judges 5:14, the leadership of Ephraim. Rabbi Aha adds that some look old without length of days and some have the days without the look, but in Abraham, whose verse the midrash is explaining, the two matched.

Rashi reads v. 1 as the land promised to Abraham, much of it not yet conquered, and Joshua too old to finish it. God's promise in v. 6, “them will I drive out,” means after Joshua's death. Joshua is to cast the lots now, and each tribe will later conquer the share that fell to it. He identifies the Shihor of v. 3 with the Nile, so the unconquered south runs from Egypt's river to Gaza.

The rabbis notice that v. 3 announces five Philistine lords and then lists six peoples. Rabbi Yonatan says there were six lords, but only five were great. Rav disagrees: the Avites were not Philistines at all but came from Teman, and the Talmud offers three plays on their name: they ruined the place they came from, they craved many gods, or they were so fearsome that all who saw them shook. Rashi also gives a simpler reading: the five lords are the five cities named, and the Avites are listed apart because they were not Philistines.

Why does v. 22 call Balaam a “soothsayer” when Numbers treats him as a prophet? Rabbi Yohanan says he began as a prophet and ended as a mere diviner, and Rav Pappa adds a proverb about a woman of noble birth who fell to low company. Rav reads the end of the verse, where Balaam dies with the Midianites he had advised, “among them that were slain,” to mean that Balaam suffered all four of the court's death penalties.

Og is “of the remnant of the giants” (v. 12), and Rashi asks what the remnant was left from. He answers from Genesis: these were the Rephaim whom Chedorlaomer and his allies struck in Ashteroth Karnaim (Genesis 14:5), and Og was a survivor of that war, long before Israel came. Og's city Ashtaroth (vv. 12, 31) lies in that same district, so the giants of Genesis and the king of Joshua share a home.

Origen reads “advanced in days” (v. 1) as a sign of spiritual maturity rather than age alone. The land that is left, the borders of the Philistines and the rest, becomes the territory Christ has still to subdue at his second coming. Joshua's unfinished work points beyond the book.

On vv. 14 and 33 Origen says the Levites received no territory because the Lord God himself is their inheritance. He applies it to those in the church who give themselves to wisdom and teaching, whose portion is God rather than land.

Eusebius describes Aroer (v. 16), once a Moabite city of the ancient Emim, as still pointed out on the brow of the mountain where the Arnon falls through its gorge toward the Dead Sea. He assigns it to Gad, as Numbers 32:34 does, though v. 16 sets it on Reuben's border. Beth-peor (v. 20) is a town of the sons of Reuben near Mount Peor, opposite Jericho, six miles above Livias. Of the Maachathites he repeats v. 13: Israel did not drive them out.

14.overview:
The division of Canaan begins. Eleazar the priest, Joshua and the heads of the tribes distribute the land by lot to nine and a half tribes; Levi receives towns but no territory, and Joseph counts as two tribes (vv. 1–5). Then the men of Judah come to Joshua at Gilgal, and Caleb speaks. He was forty when Moses sent him from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land. He brought back an honest report while the others made the people's hearts melt, and Moses swore that the ground he walked on would be his. Now, at eighty-five, he is as strong as he was then, and he asks for the hill country where the Anakim live. Joshua blesses him and gives him Hebron.

The first grant in Canaan is made before any lot is drawn. Caleb's share rests on an oath forty-five years old, and three times the chapter says why: he “wholly followed the LORD” (vv. 8, 9, 14).

14.hermeneutics:
Babylonian kings rewarded loyal soldiers with grants written on stone. A boundary stone (*kudurru*) of Nebuchadnezzar I, about 1100 BC, tells how a chariot officer named Shitti-Marduk stood by the king in the campaign against Elam. In return the king freed the towns of the officer's house, Bit-Karziyabku, from royal taxes and levies, and the stone calls down curses on anyone who would undo the grant. Caleb's grant has the same parts: a soldier's loyalty in a crisis (v. 8), a sworn promise (v. 9), and land that passes to his children. Heard against such grants, Caleb is not begging a favor in v. 12. He is presenting a sworn royal promise for payment, before the one who now speaks for the king.

Egyptian execration texts of the 19th–18th century BC wrote the names of hostile rulers on bowls and figurines that were then smashed. Among the peoples of Canaan they name is *Iy-'anaq*, with three chiefs listed by name. Many scholars connect it with the Anakim of vv. 12 and 15, though the link is debated. If it holds, the sons of Anak were a remembered people of the southern hill country, known to Egypt long before Israel, and not only the giants of the spies' fears (Numbers 13:28, 33). Caleb asks for the very ground that had frightened Israel off forty-five years before.

notes: **Wholly followed:** the phrase, Hebrew for “filled after,” comes three times: in Caleb's mouth (v. 8), in Moses' oath (v. 9), and in the narrator's verdict (v. 14). The speaker changes and the words stay the same.
**Then and now:** Caleb sets two moments side by side, the day Moses sent him and “this day.” His strength is named twice in v. 11, as it was then, so it is now.
**Hebron:** the name comes three times in vv. 13–15, ending with its older name and the giant it remembered.

The outline sets 14:1–15:63 together as Caleb and Judah's lot, but vv. 1–5 head the whole western division, which closes with matching words at 19:51. Caleb's claim comes first because he belongs to Judah, the first tribe to receive its lot (15:1). The last line, “the land had rest from war” (v. 15), repeats 11:23 and frames chs. 12–14.
**Backward and forward:** Caleb quotes the oath of Numbers 14:24 and Deuteronomy 1:36, and 15:13–19 tells how he took Hebron and Debir.

traditions.text: The rabbis use Caleb's ages to date the conquest. He was forty when sent from Kadesh in the second year after the Exodus, so he was seventy-eight when Israel crossed the Jordan in the fortieth; at eighty-five, the war had lasted seven years. The figure of seven years became the standard rabbinic length of Joshua's war, set against Josephus's shorter count (next entry).

Josephus counts differently: by his reckoning the fifth year had passed when the Canaanites were left only in their strongholds. He tells Hebron's capture after Joshua's death and says of the giants there that their bodies were so large and their faces so strange that they were terrible to see and hear. Their bones, he adds, “are still shewn to this very day.”

Why is Caleb called “the Kenezite” (v. 6) when his father was Jephunneh? Rava answers that Caleb's mother later married Kenaz, so Caleb was Kenaz's stepson and Othniel his half brother. The Talmud also reads Jephunneh not as a name but as a description: Caleb was the son who “turned away” from the spies' counsel. The same passage identifies Caleb's wife Ephrath with Miriam, so the man who claims Hebron is joined by marriage to Moses' own family.

Caleb says he brought word “as it was in mine heart” (v. 7). Rashi says it was not as it was in his mouth: while he was with the other spies he kept silent, afraid of them, and only when he came back to Moses did he say what he believed. He ties this to the “other spirit” of Numbers 14:24, and there he reads “wholly followed” as a heart filled with the intent to follow, and the land Caleb “went into” as Hebron.
traditions.cite: Rashi on Joshua 14:7; Rashi on Numbers 14:24

traditions.text: Rashi explains the arithmetic of vv. 3–4. With Levi left out there would be only eight and a half tribes west of the Jordan, so Joseph's sons Ephraim and Manasseh count as two, as Jacob had said they would (Genesis 48:5). The land is still divided among twelve.

Kirjath-arba means “city of four,” and Rashi names them: Arba, the great man of the Anakim, and his three sons Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai (Numbers 13:22). He then cites a midrash that the “great man” is Abraham himself. Because the Hittites of Hebron had honored Abraham as “a mighty prince” (Genesis 23:6), the land had rest from war for the forty years Israel spent in the wilderness.

A baraita says Joshua and Caleb took the portions of the ten spies who died. Ulla finds it in Numbers 14:38, where the two “lived still”: since Numbers 26:65 already says they survived, the rabbis read “lived” as “lived in” the others' shares. Caleb's Hebron, on this reading, is more than one man's lot; it carries the inheritance the faithless spies forfeited.

Ramban asks why the oath of Numbers 14:24, which Caleb quotes in v. 9, names Caleb and not Joshua. Caleb's reward, he says, could be stated at once: he would inherit the land he had walked. Joshua's reward was to succeed Moses, and that was not fit to announce while Moses still had years to lead. Caleb is also named first in v. 30 there because he was the first to stand up and silence the people against the spies (Numbers 13:30).

Origen reads the names. Caleb means “heart” and his father's name “conversion,” so the man who wholly followed the Lord is the converted heart. Hebron he takes to mean “conjunction” or “wedlock,” and he links it to the patriarchs buried there. He notes that Caleb, at eighty-five, is still strong for war and ready for battle, and that he asks for a mountain of great and fortified cities.

Eusebius calls Hebron the royal city of the Anakim, “founded seven years before Tanis of Egypt,” echoing Numbers 13:22. Once a metropolis of foreigners where giants lived, it became David's first capital, a Levite town and a city of refuge; in his day it was a large town twenty-two miles south of Jerusalem, where Abraham's oak and tomb were still shown. He says it was first called Arbo and later Hebron, after a son of Caleb named in Chronicles.

15.overview:
Judah's lot comes first. Its south border runs from the tip of the Salt Sea past Kadesh-barnea to the river of Egypt, its north border climbs from the Jordan's mouth past Jerusalem and Kirjath-jearim and down through Beth-shemesh to the sea. Caleb takes Hebron and drives out the three sons of Anak, and he promises his daughter Achsah to whoever captures Debir. Othniel takes it, and Achsah asks her father for springs. Judah's towns follow, district by district: the Negev, the lowland, the Philistine coast, the hill country, and the wilderness by the Dead Sea.

Jerusalem sits on the line, not inside it. The north border passes “unto the south side of the Jebusite; the same is Jerusalem” (v. 8), and the city is later counted to Benjamin (18:28). The chapter ends by admitting that Judah could not drive the Jebusites out (v. 63). After more than a hundred towns, the one city left untaken is the future capital.

15.hermeneutics:
Kingdoms in the ancient Near East kept registers of towns grouped by district, so that taxes, supplies, and labor could be assigned. Israel did the same: Solomon's twelve officers each fed the court for one month of the year (1 Kings 4:7). In 1925 Albrecht Alt argued that Judah's town list (vv. 21–62) is such a register from the kingdom of Judah, most likely in its final form under Josiah. Others, Frank Cross and G. Ernest Wright among them, dated it earlier in the monarchy. Read this way, the groups that each close with a count “with their villages” look like administrative districts, and the list shows Judah as it was later governed, set into the story of its first division.

Some of these names turn up on the kingdom's own jars. More than two thousand storage-jar handles from Judah, most from Hezekiah's reign around 700 BC, carry the stamp *lmlk*, “belonging to the king,” with one of four names: Hebron, Ziph, Socoh, or a fourth, *mmšt*, that no one has located. Hebron (v. 54), Ziph (vv. 24, 55), and Socoh (vv. 35, 48) all appear in Judah's list, though which Ziph and which Socoh is uncertain. Whole jars were found at Lachish (v. 39) in the destruction Sennacherib left there in 701 BC.

Not every name can be placed. Lachish, Azekah, Beth-shemesh, Beer-sheba, Hebron, and En-gedi are secure. Debir is not: Albright put it at Tell Beit Mirsim, and most now prefer Khirbet Rabud southwest of Hebron. Many Negev towns are known only from lists like this one, and the “city of Salt” (v. 62) has been placed at Qumran without consensus.

notes: **Two kinds of list:** the Hebrew word for border occurs 21 times in vv. 1–12, where the line is drawn; in vv. 21–62 the land is defined by its towns instead. The story of Caleb's family sits between the heading “This then was the lot” (v. 1) and the summary “This is the inheritance” (v. 20).

**Counted districts:** ten groups close with a total and “with their villages”; the Philistine cities (vv. 45–47) get no count. Twice the total and the names disagree: v. 32 says twenty-nine for about thirty-six names, and v. 36 says fourteen for fifteen.

The Judah unit (14:1–15:63) opens with the heading for the whole western division (14:1–5) and Caleb's claim to Hebron (14:6–15), then gives Judah's lot. Caleb's grant appears twice, first as a request and then as a conquest (15:13–19). Judah is placed first and Joseph next (chs. 16–17); the seven tribes surveyed at Shiloh fill the land between and beyond them.
**Forward:** Judges 1:10–15 retells Hebron, Debir, and Achsah almost word for word, and 2 Samuel 5:6–9 closes the story of v. 63 when David takes the stronghold of Zion.

traditions.text: After v. 59 the Greek has a whole district the Hebrew lacks: eleven towns, among them Tekoa, Bether, and “Ephratha, this is Bethlehem.” Most scholars think a Hebrew copyist's eye jumped from one “with their villages” to the next and dropped the group. The Greek therefore gives Bethlehem, the town of Micah 5:2, a place in Judah's list that the Hebrew and the KJV do not.

This retelling makes Kenaz, whom Joshua names only as Othniel's father (v. 17), Caleb's son. Caleb asks Joshua to give Kenaz “the territory of the three towers,” and Joshua blesses him and does so. Later Israel casts lots within Caleb's tribe for a leader, the lot falls on Kenaz, and he becomes the first ruler after Joshua, the role Judges 3:9 gives to Othniel.

The Talmud reads Kirjath-sepher, “town of the book” (v. 15), as the body of teaching forgotten in the mourning for Moses. A baraita counts 1,700 lost inferences and rulings, and Rabbi Abbahu says Othniel won them back by his sharp reasoning: that is how he “took” the town. The same passage identifies Othniel with Jabez of 1 Chronicles 4:10, whose prayer “enlarge my coast” it reads as a request for students.

The Talmud hears Achsah's dismount (v. 18) as a cry, the way a donkey cries out at an empty trough. Her “south land” becomes a house dried out of every good thing: Othniel is a man with nothing but Torah, which is water, and she asks how they will eat. Rashi follows this reading and glosses the blessing she asks for as a livelihood.

Rashi notices that v. 32 says twenty-nine cities but the list names thirty-eight by his count. His answer is that the extra nine were later taken by Simeon, and he names them from Simeon's list in 19:2–7. He also solves the fourteen of v. 36 by reading Tappuah and Enam as one town, and he marks where the line leaves Jerusalem outside Judah, in Benjamin's lot (v. 8).

Why could Judah not take Jerusalem (v. 63)? Rashi cites Rabbi Joshua ben Korha: they could have, but were not permitted, because of the oath Abraham swore to Abimelech (Genesis 21:23). He adds that “Jebusite” here names a fortress in the city called Jebus, held by people of Philistine descent. Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer, below, ties the same restraint to a different oath of Abraham's.

In this midrash the men of Jebus sold Abraham the cave of Machpelah only after he swore that his descendants would not take their city without consent. They wrote the oath on bronze images set up in the street, so Israel could not enter. These were “the blind and the lame” that David had to remove before Joab went up first and the city fell (2 Samuel 5:6–8).

Josephus describes Judah's lot as the upper part of Judea, reaching to Jerusalem, with its breadth stretching to “the lake of Sodom,” his name for the Dead Sea. He counts Ascalon and Gaza as Judah's, in line with v. 47 and Judges 1:18, though Ascalon is not named in Joshua's list. For him the coast belonged to Judah by right, whatever its later history.

Preaching on these lists, Origen admits that few hearers profit from strings of names, and he urges them not to give up. Charms work on a person who does not understand them, he says, and the names of Scripture are “stronger than any charm,” nourishing the soul even unread. He compares the listener to a charmed snake: the vipers within are weakened by Moses and Joshua whether he follows or not.

On v. 63 Origen asks how the Jebusites could live in Jerusalem “unto this day” when in his time not even Judah lived there. He reads the city as the church and the Jebusites as members whose lives are unworthy, and he joins the verse to the parable of the wheat and the tares (Matthew 13:30). Open offenders, he adds, should still be put out.

Eusebius's gazetteer of biblical places glosses Debir as the “city of letters” that Othniel took, killing the Anakim there, and notes it was later given to the priests (21:15). He gives Dannah (v. 49) the same meaning. Neither entry gives a distance from a Roman town, as Eusebius usually does, which suggests he did not know where Debir lay.

16.overview:
The lot of Joseph's sons starts at the Jordan by Jericho, climbs through the wilderness to Bethel, and runs west past lower Beth-horon to Gezer and the sea (vv. 1–4). Ephraim's own share is then marked out: a south edge from Ataroth-addar to upper Beth-horon, a north edge from Michmethah around Taanath-shiloh and Janohah down to Jericho, and a west line from Tappuah along the brook Kanah to the sea. Some of Ephraim's towns lie inside Manasseh (v. 9), and the Canaanites of Gezer stay on and serve under tribute (v. 10).

Ephraim gets borders and no list of towns. Judah's towns fill forty-two verses (15:21–62), and Benjamin's and the northern tribes' are named in chs. 18–19, but for Ephraim, as for Manasseh after it, the text gives only lines and enclaves. The one city the chapter stops to comment on is Gezer, and Gezer stayed Canaanite.

16.hermeneutics:
Gezer guarded the road that climbs from the coastal plain into the hills by way of Beth-horon (vv. 3, 5), and Egypt watched it closely. Thutmose III lists Gezer among the cities taken on his first campaign in the 15th century BC. Ten of the Amarna letters, from the 14th century, come from its rulers, swearing loyalty to Pharaoh, and Merneptah's victory stela, about 1208 BC, boasts “seized upon is Gezer.” A city with that history and those patrons was no village for a hill tribe to clear. The verse does not describe a battle; it says the Canaanites stayed and were put to forced labor.

1 Kings 9:16 records how the arrangement ended: a pharaoh took Gezer, burned it, killed its Canaanites, and gave the city as a dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife. Solomon then rebuilt it along with Hazor and Megiddo (9:15). Yigael Yadin dated a six-chambered gate at Gezer to Solomon; others, Israel Finkelstein among them, date it later, and there is no consensus. Either way, the “unto this day” of v. 10 looks out from a time when Canaanites still lived in Gezer.

Gezer is also one of the surest identifications in the land. Thirteen boundary stones cut in the rock around Tell Jezer, from the late 2nd or 1st century BC, read “boundary of Gezer” in Hebrew, most with a Greek name beside it. The rest of Ephraim's line is harder. The two Beth-horons survive in the village names Beit Ur al-Fauqa and al-Tahta, and Taanath-shiloh and Janohah are tied to Ta'na and Yanun east of Shechem, but Michmethah, Naarath, and Ataroth-addar are not securely placed.

notes: **Drawn twice:** the southern line of vv. 1–3 (Jericho, Bethel, Ataroth, Beth-horon) is traced again for Ephraim in v. 5, and again in reverse as Benjamin's north border in 18:12–13. The Hebrew word for border occurs eight times in ten verses.

**A closing note:** like Judah's lot (15:63), Ephraim's ends with people who were not driven out and remain “unto this day” (v. 10). Manasseh's lot will end the same way (17:12–13), so all three of the first allotments close on unfinished conquest.

The Joseph unit (16:1–17:18) gives one lot to Joseph's two sons and then divides it. Chapter 16 opens with the joint line (vv. 1–4) and gives Ephraim's share; ch. 17 gives Manasseh's and ends with Joseph's complaint that one lot is too small. Ephraim, the younger son, is placed first, as Jacob placed him first (Genesis 48:19–20).
**Forward:** Judges 1:29 repeats that Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites of Gezer, and 1 Kings 9:16 tells how a pharaoh finally emptied the city and gave it to Solomon.

traditions.text: Jubilees tells of a war long before Joshua on this same ground. The kings of Tappuah, Shiloh, Gaash, Beth-horon and other towns of the hills attack Jacob's sons near Shechem, and Jacob defeats them, puts them under tribute, and builds Robel and Tamnatares, a form of Timnath-serah, Joshua's later town (19:50). Places on Ephraim's border are already, in this telling, Jacob's conquest and his tributaries, so the tribute of v. 10 has a precedent in the patriarch's own day.

The Greek version extends v. 10. After “unto this day” it continues: until Pharaoh king of Egypt went up, took the city, burned it, destroyed its Canaanites, and gave it as a dowry to his daughter. The added words come from 1 Kings 9:16, so the Greek reader learns in Joshua how the Canaanites of Gezer finally left; Augustine, below, noticed that the Hebrew lacks the line. The Greek also splits Taanath-shiloh in v. 6 into two places, Thenasa and Selles.

Josephus summarizes Ephraim's lot as running in length from the Jordan to Gezer, and in breadth from Bethel to “the great plain,” the Jezreel valley to the north. His summary keeps the chapter's two fixed points, the Jordan and Gezer, and adds a northern limit that the text leaves to Manasseh. He says nothing about the Canaanites who stayed.

Rabbi Avdimi bar Hasa found a hint of Shiloh's fall in Taanath-shiloh (v. 6). He hears the name as “mourning of Shiloh”: it was the place from which anyone who saw the sanctuary after its destruction would moan, because offerings once eaten within sight of Shiloh could be eaten there no longer. A boundary marker on Ephraim's north side becomes a memorial of the tabernacle's loss. The same page goes on to debate whether Shiloh itself stood in Joseph's land or on a strip belonging to Benjamin.

Rashi explains why Joseph's lot begins where it does: it fell along the northern edge of what Joshua had already conquered, leaving a wide stretch between Judah and Joseph for the remaining tribes, as Benjamin's lot later shows (18:11). On v. 9 he explains the “separate cities” as Ephraimite towns cut off from its own territory and swallowed up inside Manasseh's.

Verse 2 says the line goes out “from Beth-el to Luz,” though Genesis 28:19 says Luz was Bethel's old name. Rashi concludes that there were two places: Jacob's Bethel, which was Luz, and another Bethel near Ai. He takes the wording of this verse as his proof that the names could not mean one city.

Augustine quotes the Septuagint's longer v. 10 and asks whether the line about Pharaoh is a prophecy. He doubts it, since the book was thought to be written close to the events and a prophet would announce greater things. Checking the translation made from the Hebrew, he found the line missing and judged it an addition by the Seventy from the books of Kings, as with the line on the rebuilding of Jericho (6:26).

Origen sets v. 10 beside 15:63. Ephraim means “fruitfulness,” he says, and the Canaanite of Gezer is the restless, shifting temptation that never stops living alongside a soul that grows. When such a person troubles the church and cannot be put out, he advises Paul's counsel to withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly (2 Thessalonians 3:6). He ends by praying that God will subject both Jebusite and Canaanite.

In the next homily Origen reads v. 10 with 17:13 and 17:18 as three stages: first the Canaanite only pays tribute, then he serves, and at last he is destroyed, as the flesh is first taxed, then mastered, then put to death (Colossians 3:5). He takes Gezer to mean “constriction,” and the Greek text's Pharaoh, who takes the city as his daughter's dowry, as the king of sin who carries off a soul that lives by the flesh.

Procopius follows Origen's line: Ephraim is fruitful yet cannot expel the Canaanite, and so it is with the church and with every soul, none of which stays pure in this life. He pairs the Canaanites of Gezer with the Jebusites of Jerusalem (15:63) as one lesson. Only those who call on God, he says, can drive such things out.

17.overview:
Manasseh, Joseph's firstborn, holds land on both sides of the Jordan. Machir's line already has Gilead and Bashan (v. 1), and the other clans, Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher, and Shemida, receive land to the west. Zelophehad's five daughters remind Eleazar and Joshua of the Lord's command to Moses, and they are given their share (vv. 3–6). Manasseh's line runs from Michmethah by Shechem to the brook Kanah and the sea, and it claims Beth-shean, Megiddo, and other cities whose Canaanites it cannot drive out. Joseph's tribes then complain that one lot is too small, and Joshua sends them to clear the forest.

The daughters are counted as shares. Ten portions fall to Manasseh west of the Jordan “because the daughters of Manasseh had an inheritance among his sons” (v. 6). The ruling of Numbers 27 now appears on the map.

17.hermeneutics:
In 1910 excavators at Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom, found about a hundred potsherds inscribed in ink in the 8th century BC. They record deliveries of aged wine and fine oil, and many name the district they came from: Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shemida, Hoglah, and Noah. The first four are sons' clans in v. 2; the last two are daughters of Zelophehad in v. 3. Centuries after this allotment the clan names of Manasseh, the daughters' among them, were still the names of working districts around the capital. The daughters in vv. 3–6 are people in the story and places on the later map.

The cities Manasseh could not take (v. 11) were the strongest in the north. When Thutmose III of Egypt marched on Megiddo in the 15th century BC, his annals weigh the road by way of Taanach against a narrow pass, and after a seven-month siege list 924 chariots among the spoil. Megiddo and Taanach, Beth-shean and Dor sat on the plains where chariots could move, which is the complaint of v. 16. “Chariots of iron” probably means chariots with iron fittings, since iron was still scarce.

Those valley cities are securely located: Beth-shean at Tel Beth Shean, Megiddo at Tell el-Mutesellim, Taanach at Tell Ti'innik, Ibleam at Khirbet Bel'ameh, Dor on the coast at Tel Dor. The hill-country line is not. Michmethah and En-tappuah are disputed, and no one is sure what the “three countries” of v. 11 were.

notes: **Daughters:** the Hebrew word for daughter occurs ten times. Three refer to Zelophehad's daughters (vv. 3, 6); the other seven are the dependent “towns” of the Canaanite cities (vv. 11, 16), which Hebrew calls a city's daughters.

**Turned back on them:** Joseph calls itself a “great people” and asks why it has “one lot” (v. 14). Joshua repeats “great people” twice (vv. 15, 17) and answers “thou shalt not have one lot only” (v. 17), so their own words become the reason they must clear the forest and drive out the Canaanites.

Chapter 17 completes the Joseph unit (16:1–17:18). The joint line of 16:1–4 was split, Ephraim's share first; here Manasseh's share and the enclaves each tribe holds in the other's land (16:9; 17:8–9) show how tangled the two remained. The unit ends with the people of Joseph asking for more, just before the seven remaining tribes are told they have been slow to take any (18:3).
**Backward:** Numbers 27:1–11 and 36:1–12 set the rule that Zelophehad's daughters inherit and must marry within the tribe. **Forward:** Judges 1:27–28 lists the same unconquered cities.

traditions.text: A thematic link. Alma 10:3 traces Lehi to Manasseh, the tribe whose lot is drawn here, yet says he came out of Jerusalem, far south of Manasseh's border. The Bible itself records people of Manasseh going over to Judah under King Asa and coming to Jerusalem in Hezekiah's day (2 Chronicles 15:9; 30:11). Lehi's family, in this reading, is one of those branches of Joseph that left its allotted hills.

The Talmud works out the ten portions of v. 5. Six go to the six clans named in v. 2, and four to Zelophehad's daughters, who took their father's share as one who left Egypt, a double share in their grandfather Hepher's estate since Zelophehad was firstborn, and an uncle's share. The sages then argue whether the land was divided among those who left Egypt or those who entered it, and how the numbers change under each view. Rashi on v. 5 adopts the six-and-four count and adds that the daughters did not each become a clan of her own; they simply held four shares.

Why record Joseph's complaint at all, when it was not granted? To teach caution about the evil eye. Joshua's “get thee up to the wood country” (v. 15) is read as advice to hide a large tribe in the forests, out of envious sight. Joseph's descendants answer that the evil eye has no power over them, citing Jacob's blessing of Joseph “by a well” (Genesis 49:22), read as “above the eye.”

Rashi assigns the complaint to Manasseh and explains “the LORD hath blessed me hitherto” (v. 14) by the census figures. Manasseh grew from 32,200 men in the first count to 52,700 in the second (Numbers 1:35; 26:34), no other tribe grew as much. A share fixed for the smaller tribe no longer fit. On v. 1 he adds that Machir, as Manasseh's firstborn, took his portion first, in Moses' lifetime, east of the Jordan.

On Joshua's answer, Rashi has him say that a numerous people has the strength to cut down forests and build towns there. The wooded hill country “is fit only for a great people,” and the Canaanite with iron chariots is a foe none of the other tribes could face, but Joseph can. What looks like a refusal becomes, in Rashi, a compliment and a commission.

The obscure “three countries” at the end of v. 11 the Targum renders as three districts. Rashi ties them to Dor, whose region Joshua names elsewhere with a closely related word (11:2; 12:23), and explains the phrase as the three districts that belonged to Dor and its towns. Modern translators are still unsure of the word.

Josephus gives the western half of Manasseh the land from the Jordan to the city of Dora on the coast, with its breadth at “Bethshan, which is now called Scythopolis.” His two landmarks are the coastal and valley cities of v. 11, the very places the chapter says Manasseh could not take. Eusebius, below, uses the same Roman name for Beth-shean.

Origen applies Joseph's request to his hearers: if we are a numerous people whom the Lord has blessed, we too must go up into the forest and clear out the Perizzites and the Rephaim. He reads Perizzites as “fruitfulness,” here the bad fruit to be cut away, and Rephaim as weakened “mothers,” powers of the soul that need cleansing, not destruction. The Canaanite's horse and iron (v. 16) are the weapons Israel never trusts.

traditions.source: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis
traditions.text: Ephrem reads v. 13 as the fulfillment of Noah's words, “Canaan shall be his servant” (Genesis 9:26). Japheth grew strong in the north and west, God dwelt in the tents of Shem through Abraham, and Canaan became a servant when Israel under Joshua put its leaders to tribute. The forced labor of this chapter closes a story begun after the Flood, and Ephrem reads it as history, without allegory.

Eusebius lists Beth-shean, Taanach, and Ibleam each with the note that Manasseh could not expel their people. Beth-shean is “now Scythopolis, a famous city,” whose name he explains as “house of enmity,” and he recalls that Deborah fought Sisera at Taanach (Judges 5:19). In his day these were living places, a reminder to his readers of how long the Canaanite cities of v. 11 outlasted Manasseh's claim.

18.overview:
Israel gathers at Shiloh and sets up the tent of meeting there, with the land subdued before them. Seven tribes still have no inheritance, and Joshua asks how long they will be slack. He has each tribe choose three men to walk through the land and describe it in seven parts; they come back to Shiloh with a book, and Joshua casts lots for them before the LORD (vv. 1–10). The first lot falls to Benjamin, a strip between Judah and Joseph from the Jordan to Kirjath-jearim. Its borders are traced and its towns listed, Jericho, Bethel, Gibeon, and Jebusi, “which is Jerusalem,” among them.

The land is put in writing before it is handed out. The men “described it by cities into seven parts in a book” (v. 9), and the Hebrew verb behind “describe” is the ordinary verb for writing. For the last seven tribes a written survey comes first, and the lot is cast over a document.

18.hermeneutics:
Shiloh was a real hill-country center at the time the book describes. Danish teams dug there from 1926 to 1932, and Israel Finkelstein excavated from 1981 to 1984. Near the top of the tell he found Iron Age I pillared buildings holding collared-rim storage jars and cult objects, more than twenty grain silos, and a burned layer across the site that radiocarbon puts about 1050 BC, a fit for Shiloh's ruin in Jeremiah 7:12 and Psalm 78:60. The summit, where a sanctuary would most likely have stood, is bare bedrock, so the tent of v. 1 has left no trace. What the ground does show is a storage complex suited to a shrine that drew pilgrims.

Writing land down before dividing it was ordinary practice for a state. The Wilbour Papyrus, a ten-meter Egyptian roll from about 1145 BC, records plot after plot of farmland along some 140 kilometers of Middle Egypt, with the holder's name and occupation and the grain expected from it. Joshua's survey of v. 9 belongs to the same world: men walk the land, list it by towns, and bring back a document on which the division can be made.

Shiloh itself is secure. Judges 21:19 places it north of Bethel, east of the road to Shechem and south of Lebonah, which fits Khirbet Seilun, where the old name survives. Among Benjamin's towns Jericho, Bethel, Gibeon (el-Jib), and Ramah (er-Ram) are generally accepted; Mizpeh is disputed between Tell en-Nasbeh and Nebi Samwil, and places such as Zelah, Eleph, and Taralah are unknown.

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence, from the survey at Shiloh to the first of its lots.
notes: **Write, Shiloh, before the LORD:** the Hebrew verb for writing occurs five times in vv. 4–9, Shiloh four times in vv. 1–10, and “before the LORD” three times (vv. 6, 8, 10). The survey is human work, and the lot that follows is placed in the LORD's presence.

**Borrowed lines:** Benjamin's north border repeats Joseph's south line (16:1–3) and its south border repeats Judah's north line (15:5–9), traced the other way, from Kirjath-jearim east to the Salt Sea. Benjamin's lot is made of the edges of its neighbors'.

The Shiloh unit (18:1–19:51) opens and closes with the tent at Shiloh (18:1; 19:51) and holds the seven remaining lots, Benjamin's first. The move from Gilgal to Shiloh marks a turn: the war camp by the Jordan becomes a sanctuary in the hills. Joshua's rebuke (v. 3) echoes the LORD's words in 13:1 that very much land remains.

**Forward:** Shiloh hosts the Levites' claim (21:2) and the eastern tribes' departure (22:9), and it is still the LORD's house in Samuel's childhood (1 Samuel 1:3, 24), until the ark is taken from there to battle and lost (1 Samuel 4:3–11).

traditions.text: A thematic link. Writing to the Saints in Missouri about inheritances in Zion, Joseph Smith records the Lord's promise to send one who would set in order the house of God and “arrange by lot the inheritances of the saints.” Those inheritances belong to people whose names, with their fathers' and children's, are enrolled in the book of God's law, and the revelation charges the Lord's clerk to keep that record; those not found written there receive none. Lot and book stand together, as they do at Shiloh (vv. 6, 9).

The Mishnah describes the sanctuary at Shiloh as neither tent nor temple: it had no roof of wood or stone, only a stone building below with the tabernacle's curtains spread over it. The Talmud uses this to reconcile Scripture's calling it a “house” (1 Samuel 1:24) and a “tent” (Psalm 78:60). Rashi brings the same description to v. 1.
traditions.cite: m. Zevachim 14:6; b. Zevachim 118a; Rashi on 18:1

traditions.text: How long did the tent stay where v. 1 puts it? A baraita counts back from the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1: thirty-nine in the wilderness, fourteen at Gilgal, and fifty-seven at Nob and Gibeon. What remains is 369 years at Shiloh, from Joshua's day until Eli's death, when the ark was lost and Shiloh destroyed (1 Samuel 4).

Where exactly did the tent stand? One teacher held that God's presence rested only in Benjamin's land, at Shiloh, Nob, Gibeon, and the Temple, citing Moses' blessing that the LORD dwells “between his shoulders” (Deuteronomy 33:12). Rav Yosef objected that Psalm 78:67 puts Shiloh in Joseph's tent. The answer offered is a tongue of Joseph's land jutting into Benjamin's, on which the tabernacle stood.

Rashi reads v. 1 causally: once the tabernacle was fixed, the land was easy to conquer before them. On v. 4 he insists that the seven parts were not equal, but sized to each tribe as Numbers 26:54 commands. And he observes that wherever Judah's border “went up,” Benjamin's “went down” (v. 15), since one is traced east to west and the other west to east.

Josephus says Joshua chose Shiloh for the tabernacle “because of the beauty of its situation,” until a temple could be built. He calls Benjamin's lot the narrowest of all, bounded in breadth by Jerusalem and Bethel, and explains why: it held Jericho and Jerusalem, the best land. Size followed value, a principle he applies to the whole division.

A baraita says Joshua attached ten conditions to the land when he divided it among the tribes. Anyone might graze flocks in woods, gather brushwood and wild plants, take water from a spring, and fish the Sea of Galilee without blocking boats; a traveler lost in vineyards could cut his way out; and an unclaimed corpse was to be buried where it lay. Private shares, on this view, came with public rights.

Preaching at Pisidian Antioch, Paul compresses Joshua into one clause: God destroyed seven nations in Canaan and “divided their land to them by lot.” The allotment at Shiloh becomes one step in a history that runs from the Exodus through the judges and Saul to David and then to Jesus. Paul's summary keeps the detail of the lot.

In his memorial of the Roman widow Paula, Jerome lists the holy places she visited, among them Shiloh, “where a ruined altar is still shown today.” He recalls in the same breath that Benjamin carried off wives there (Judges 21:20–23), comparing it to Rome's legend of the Sabine women. For Christian pilgrims of the 4th century, Shiloh was a site to visit, not only a name.

Eusebius lists Shiloh in Ephraim as the place where the ark and tabernacle stayed until Samuel's time, twelve miles from Neapolis, the Roman city at Shechem, in the district of Akrabattine. His distance and direction point to Khirbet Seilun, the same site that Judges 21:19 indicates.

Augustine takes v. 28's “Jebusi, which is Jerusalem” as a picture of conversion. Unlike Cain's city, built where none stood, Jerusalem was built on the site of Jebus: the old city was captured and thrown down, and a new one raised, named “vision of peace.” So every child of Adam belongs first to an old city, and must have the old self thrown down to be built new.

19.overview:
The last six lots come out in turn. Simeon's towns, Beer-sheba, Hormah, Ziklag and others, lie inside Judah, because Judah's share was too large for it (vv. 1–9). Zebulun, Issachar, Asher, and Naphtali receive the north, from the Jezreel valley and Mount Tabor to Carmel, Tyre, Sidon, and the Sea of Chinnereth. Dan's lot runs from Zorah down to the coast by Joppa, but it proves too small, and the Danites take Leshem in the far north and rename it Dan (v. 47). The division closes at Shiloh before the LORD.

Joshua is served last. The man who cast every lot receives a share only after all the tribes have theirs, and the people give it to him “according to the word of the LORD” (vv. 49–50). He asks for Timnath-serah in the hills of Ephraim, and then he builds the town himself.

19.hermeneutics:
Simeon's list includes Sharuhen (v. 6), a name also known from Egypt. The tomb autobiography of Ahmose son of Ebana, an Egyptian soldier, records that after the Hyksos capital Avaris fell, about 1550 BC, Sharuhen in southwest Canaan was besieged for three years before it was taken. Its site is disputed: Tell el-Far'ah (South), Tell el-Ajjul, and Tel Haror all have defenders. Either way, Simeon's short list of desert towns includes a fortress that once held off an Egyptian army.

Dan's new city was old. Laish appears in Egyptian execration texts of the Middle Kingdom, which cursed enemy rulers by name, and in the list of Thutmose III. At Tel Dan the excavators found a mud-brick gate with three intact arches, built about 1750 BC, and above the Bronze Age city a later village of the early Iron Age. A Greek and Aramaic stone of the 3rd or 2nd century BC, found in 1976, records a vow “to the god who is in Dan,” fixing the site. The Danites of v. 47 took over a city that had already stood for centuries.

The northern lists mix certain and unknown places. Hazor, Kedesh, Chinnereth, Shunem, Jezreel, Achzib, Tyre, Sidon, and Joppa are located; Hammath is the hot springs south of Tiberias. Many border points, such as Sarid, Dabbasheth, Neiel, and Lakum, are known only from this chapter. Joshua's Timnath-serah is usually placed at Khirbet Tibnah in the hills northwest of Bethel, with the village Kifl Haris as an alternative.

notes: **Numbered lots:** each lot is counted as it comes out, second through seventh (vv. 1, 10, 17, 24, 32, 40), and each closes with the same line, “This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of …” (vv. 8, 16, 23, 31, 39, 48).

**A wider frame:** 19:51 names Eleazar, Joshua, and the heads of the fathers, the same three parties named when the division began (14:1). The whole western division, chs. 14–19, sits inside those two notices, and Joshua's own share comes just before the last one.

Chapter 19 completes the Shiloh unit (18:1–19:51) and the land division begun in 14:1. Joshua's own inheritance seals it, as Caleb's opened it (14:6–15): the two faithful spies of Numbers 14 receive the first and last personal grants. The Levites' cities (ch. 21) and the cities of refuge (ch. 20) are drawn from the tribal lands just assigned.
**Forward:** Judges 18 tells the Danite migration of v. 47 in full, and Joshua is buried in his own town, Timnath-serah (24:30).

traditions.text: The Greek expands Dan's story with material close to Judges 1:34–35: the Amorites pressed Dan into the hills and would not let them come down to the valley. Dan then attacks “Lachis,” not Leshem, and calls it Lasendan. A further line adds that the Amorites stayed in Elom and Salamin until the hand of Ephraim made them tributaries.

The Talmud matches Naphtali's fortified cities (v. 35) to the towns of its own day. Hammath is the hot springs near Tiberias, Chinnereth is Ginosar, whose fruit is sweet as the sound of a harp (*kinnor*), and Rakkath is argued over, Sepphoris or Tiberias, until Tiberias wins. Rabbi Yitzhak adds that Leshem, which Dan took (v. 47), is Paneas.

The same page has Zebulun complain that its brothers received fields and vineyards while it got mountains, seas, and rivers. God answers that all Israel will need Zebulun for the *hilazon*, the sea creature that yields the blue dye for fringes, reading Moses' blessing of “treasures hid in the sand” (Deuteronomy 33:19). Anyone who took these goods without paying, the sages add, would not prosper.

Rashi explains “the second lot” (v. 1) as second among the seven drawn at Shiloh, Benjamin's being the first, since Judah and Joseph already had theirs. On v. 9 he glosses Judah's share as more than was fitting for it. On v. 13 he identifies Gath-hepher as the town of Jonah son of Amittai (2 Kings 14:25), a link Eusebius also makes.

Rashi says the war against Leshem (v. 47) came later, in the days of Othniel and of Micah's image, as told in Judges 18, and that Leshem is the Laish of that story. He reads “went out too little for them” as Dan holding part of its lot here and receiving another far from its border, with other tribes between.

Josephus gives the northern lots broad strokes: Zebulun to the lake of Gennesareth, Naphtali east as far as Damascus and Upper Galilee to Lebanon and the springs of the Jordan, Dan from Azotus to Dora on the coast. Later he tells how Canaanite chariots drove the Danites into the hills, so they sent five men north and built Dan near “the fountains of the lesser Jordan.”

Origen dwells on Joshua's humility. The man who gave Judah, Ephraim, Manasseh, and Caleb their land, and sent the surveyors, reserved himself for last, and did not even claim his own lot but received it from the people. Origen reads it as the precept of Sirach 3:18, the greater you are, the more humble yourself.

Eusebius found the overlap between Simeon's towns and Judah's (vv. 1–9) and refused to move either. Since Judah excelled in war, he suggests, it gained a share of other tribes' land in the final description, and Scripture plainly says Simeon lived in Judah's midst. Beer-sheba in his day was a large village with a Roman garrison, twenty miles south of Hebron.

Two of Eusebius's northern entries tie Joshua's lists to later Scripture. Kanah in Asher, “near Sidon the Great” (v. 28), he takes to be the Cana where Jesus changed water into wine, the home of Nathanael. Gath-hepher in Zebulun (v. 13) he calls the home of Jonah the prophet, as Rashi does.

Matthew places Jesus' new home, Capernaum, “in the borders of Zabulon and Nephthalim,” and quotes Isaiah 9:1–2 on the land of these two tribes seeing a great light. The northern lots of this chapter become the setting of the ministry's first preaching.

Augustine comments on the Septuagint's line that the Amorites in Elom and Salamin became Ephraim's tributaries (v. 48a). Sparing them was already against the Lord's command, he says, and it happened while Joshua lived but was too old to lead in battle. He links it to 11:20, where God hardened the Canaanites' hearts so they would fight and not be spared.

Warning a former student about borrowing pagan learning, Origen recalls Jeroboam's two golden calves, one at Bethel and one at Dan (1 Kings 12:29). He adds that Dan's boundaries, as the Book of Joshua shows, are “farthest off, and near those of the Gentiles.” Dan's move to the edge of the land (v. 47) becomes an image of ideas drifting toward the world outside.

20.overview:
With the land divided, the LORD tells Joshua to appoint the cities of refuge he had commanded through Moses. A person who kills someone by accident may flee to one of them. He stands at the city gate, explains his case to the elders, and they take him in and give him a place to live; they must not hand him over to the avenger of blood. He stays until the congregation has judged him and the high priest of those days has died, then goes home. Israel sets apart Kedesh, Shechem, and Hebron west of the Jordan, matching Bezer, Ramoth, and Golan to the east, for Israelites and resident foreigners alike.

The chapter stitches together the two earlier refuge laws. Verse 3 uses Numbers' word for an accident and Deuteronomy's phrase “unwittingly” side by side, and the hearing at the gate before the elders (v. 4) appears in neither of them.

20.hermeneutics:
In the ancient Near East the family of the dead usually decided what happened to a killer. The Hittite Edict of Telipinu (about 1500 BC) says that in a case of bloodshed the “lord of the blood” chooses: if he says the killer shall die, he dies; if he says he shall pay, he pays. Middle Assyrian law likewise hands a killer to the victim's next of kin, who may put him to death or take compensation. Joshua 20 takes that choice away from the kin. The avenger may pursue, but the elders “shall not deliver the slayer up into his hand” (v. 5), and the congregation, not the family, decides the case (v. 6).

The hearing takes place “at the entering of the gate” (v. 4), and excavated gates show what that looked like. At Tel Dan, Avraham Biran's team found in the courtyard between the outer and inner gates of the Iron Age city a long stone bench, which the excavators call the “bench of the elders,” beside a canopied structure and a row of standing stones. A fugitive arriving at such a gate would tell his story in public, to the men seated there, before he was let inside.

Asylum in the ancient world clung to holy places, and many scholars note that the three western refuges were old sanctuary towns. Shechem had its sanctuary and sacred oak (24:26), Hebron its altar from Abraham's day (Genesis 13:18), and Kedesh means “holy place.” The verb in v. 7 plays on that name: Israel “sanctified” (KJV “appointed”) Kedesh. The refuge stays attached to sacred towns, but the protection now comes from a hearing and a rule of law.

Six cities named, three and three
Summary: for all Israel and the stranger

notes: **Two laws woven together:** Numbers' word *bishgagah*, “unawares” (Numbers 35:11, 15), opens and closes the chapter (vv. 3, 9). Deuteronomy's “unwittingly” and “hated him not beforetime” (Deuteronomy 19:4, 6) stand in vv. 3 and 5. The congregation, the high priest, and the word for refuge come from Numbers; Deuteronomy 19 has none of the three.
**The avenger** of blood is named three times (vv. 3, 5, 9), each time as the one the slayer is kept from.
**Wordplay:** the verb of v. 7, “sanctified,” shares its root with the first city named, Kedesh.

The allotment to the tribes ends at 19:51. Chapters 20–21 then set aside towns from every tribe's share for two purposes: six refuges and forty-eight Levite towns, the refuges among them (21:13, 21, 27, 32, 38). The section closes with the summary of 21:43–45 before the farewell chapters begin.

**Backward and forward:** the chapter carries out Numbers 35:9–15 and Deuteronomy 19:1–3, completing the three that Moses set apart east of the Jordan (Deuteronomy 4:41–43). Later accounts name no one who fled to these towns; Joab and Adonijah seize the horns of the altar instead (1 Kings 1:50; 2:28).

traditions.text: A thematic link. A revelation on the gathering speaks of the New Jerusalem as “a city of refuge,” a place of safety where the glory of the Lord will dwell. Those who will not take up the sword against their neighbor flee to it for safety, as the slayer of v. 3 flees to a city the avenger may not enter.

The main Greek text of Joshua, Codex Vaticanus, which Brenton translated in 1844, has no vv. 4–6: no hearing at the gate and no stay until the high priest's death. It keeps only the one Greek word for an accident in v. 3 and adds there that the slayer may not be killed until he stands before the congregation for judgment. Codex Alexandrinus has the missing verses. Many textual scholars think the Greek preserves an older, shorter form of the chapter, to which the Hebrew added the procedure from Deuteronomy.

Josephus folds this chapter into the gift of towns to the Levites. Joshua, too old to finish the conquest, tells the tribes to give the Levites thirty-eight cities and assigns three of them to those fleeing an avenger, because he was anxious that nothing Moses ordained be neglected. He names them Hebron of Judah, Shechem of Ephraim, and Cadesh, “a place of the upper Galilee.”

A baraita says Moses' three cities and Joshua's three lay “like two rows in a vineyard”: Hebron opposite Bezer, Shechem opposite Ramoth, and Kedesh opposite Golan. Why put a refuge in the middle of the land, close to everyone? Abaye answers that killers were common around Shechem too, reading Hosea 6:9, where the Hebrew has priests murdering on the road toward Shechem (KJV “by consent”).

The rabbis drew a profile of a proper refuge from this chapter. It must be a middling town, neither a village nor a great city, with water, markets, and enough people, and no nets or ropes may be sold there, so that an avenger has no reason to come. The Talmud even asks whether Kedesh qualifies, since Joshua 19:37 lists a Kedesh among the fortified cities, and answers that there were two places of that name. If a student is exiled, his teacher goes with him, because the law says the slayer must “live” there.

Rabbi Elazar takes v. 4 literally: a slayer is not admitted to a town that has no elders, because he must speak his case “in the ears of the elders of that city.” Others treat the hearing as the proper way to do it but not a condition of refuge. The same discussion notices that vv. 1–2 use the harsher Hebrew verb for speaking three times, and one opinion holds the sharper tone was a rebuke because Joshua had delayed setting the cities apart.

Did the slayer pay rent to his Levite hosts? Rabbi Judah said yes and Rabbi Meir said no, and the Talmud explains that in the six named cities all agreed he lived free. The medieval commentator David Kimhi (Radak) reads v. 4, “give him a place,” the same way. Radak also notes that the refuges come only now, after the land is divided, because the law tied them to Israel's settling in it.
traditions.cite: m. Makkot 2:8; b. Makkot 13a; Radak on Joshua 20:1, 4

traditions.text: Verse 6 says the slayer “shall dwell in that city,” and the Mishnah makes the stay absolute. He may not leave even to give testimony, and even if Israel needs him as badly as it needed Joab, the commander of David's army, he stays. If the verdict came when there was no high priest, or if the dead man was the high priest himself, he never leaves; as the Mishnah puts it, there is his home, his death, and his burial.

Rashi reads v. 6 as two stages. The slayer stands before the congregation for judgment; if acquitted he goes free, and if sentenced to exile he returns to his city of refuge and stays until the high priest dies. For v. 8 he adds that the eastern cities had been set apart already in Moses' day, citing Deuteronomy 4:43.

Eusebius' gazetteer of biblical places marks each of the six as a priestly city of refuge and fixes it on the map of his day. Kedesh is now Kudissos, twenty miles from Tyre near Paneas; Golan is still a large village in Batanaea that gives its name to the district; Ramoth lies fifteen miles west of Philadelphia (Amman). He identifies Bezer with Bostra, the metropolis of Arabia, and says Shechem is where Joseph's bones are buried.

21.overview:
The heads of the Levite families come to Eleazar, Joshua, and the tribal leaders at Shiloh and claim the towns Moses promised them. The tribes give them forty-eight towns with their pasture lands, assigned by lot to the three Levite clans. The priests, Aaron's descendants within the clan of Kohath, draw first and receive thirteen towns from Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin, Hebron among them. The other Kohathites receive ten, Gershon thirteen, and Merari twelve. The six cities of refuge are counted within the forty-eight. The chapter then closes the whole division of the land: the LORD gave Israel the land he swore to the fathers, and rest on every side.

That closing summary claims everything was fulfilled: “There failed not ought of any good thing” (v. 45). Yet the book has already said that “very much land” remained (13:1) and that Canaanites still lived in Gezer (16:10), a town on this very list (v. 21).

historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. The Talmud credits Joshua, with the account of his death added by Eleazar and Phinehas; many scholars see the book as part of a larger history compiled in the 7th–6th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Joshua's lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th century BC, drawing on older sources. Many date the town list itself to the monarchy (see Hermeneutics).

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: At Shiloh after the tribal allotment: about 1400 BC by the reckoning from 1 Kings 6:1; many scholars prefer the late 13th or 12th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The request is made at Shiloh (v. 2); the towns lie in every tribe's territory, from Hebron and Beth-shemesh in the south to Kedesh in Galilee and Golan in Bashan.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Numbers 35:1–8 (the command); 1 Chronicles 6:54–81 (the same list, with spelling and some name differences).

21.hermeneutics:
Several towns on the list were not Israelite, by the Bible's own account, until much later. Gezer (v. 21) kept its Canaanite population (16:10; Judges 1:29) until a pharaoh captured and burned it and gave it as a dowry to his daughter, Solomon's wife (1 Kings 9:16). Taanach (v. 25) also held out (17:11–12; Judges 1:27). W. F. Albright and others concluded that the list fits the united monarchy of David and Solomon, the only time every town on it was in Israel's hands. Yehezkel Kaufmann took the opposite view: it is a very early plan for the Levites, drawn up when the tribes dispersed and never fully carried out. Julius Wellhausen thought it a late memory of the many priestly towns of old. There is no consensus.

Benjamin Mazar went further and read the Levites as an arm of the royal administration, settled in frontier and provincial towns to manage crown estates and collect revenue. Chronicles supports at least part of that picture. In David's fortieth year Levites of the Hebron family were set over Israel west of the Jordan and over Reuben, Gad, and half Manasseh “for every matter pertaining to God, and affairs of the king” (1 Chronicles 26:30–32). The list also leaves out Israel's best-known shrines: Shiloh, where the request is made, Bethel, Jerusalem, and Nob, later called “the city of the priests” (1 Samuel 22:19). Whatever its date, the scheme spreads the Levites among the tribes instead of gathering them at sanctuaries.
