The four lots summarized: 13, 10, 13, and 12 towns
Aaron's sons: thirteen towns from Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin
The other Kohathites: ten towns in the center
Gershon: thirteen towns in the north and Bashan
Merari: twelve towns in Zebulun, Reuben, and Gad
Total: forty-eight towns with their pasture lands
The land given, rest granted, every promise kept

structure.summary: Summary, then detail: the four lots are announced (vv. 4–7) and then listed town by town in the same order (vv. 9–40), framed by the request and the closing summary.

open.text: The Levites ask for the towns Moses commanded

close.text: All the land given; not one good word failed

notes: **The arithmetic:** 13 + 10 + 13 + 12 = 48 (v. 41). The total works only with vv. 36–37, Reuben's four towns. Those two verses are missing from many Hebrew manuscripts and early printed editions; the Leningrad-based text used here, the Septuagint, and 1 Chronicles 6:78–79 have them.
**Refuge formula:** “to be a city of refuge for the slayer” marks Hebron, Shechem, Golan, Kedesh, and Ramoth (vv. 13, 21, 27, 32, 38). Bezer, the sixth refuge of 20:8, appears in v. 36 without it.
**Closing echo:** “there failed not” (v. 45) is literally “there fell not a word,” the verb Joshua repeats twice in 23:14.

The last chapter of the allotment (chs. 13–21). Levi alone had no tribal territory (13:14, 33; 14:3–4), so its towns are taken out of everyone else's, and vv. 43–45 close the whole division of the land, not just this list. Chapter 22 then sends the eastern tribes home.

**Backward and forward:** Jacob's word that Levi would be scattered in Israel (Genesis 49:7) becomes a settled network of towns. Two of the priests' towns reappear later: Anathoth, where Solomon banishes the priest Abiathar (1 Kings 2:26) and Jeremiah's family lives (Jeremiah 1:1), and Beth-shemesh, where the ark returns from the Philistines (1 Samuel 6:13–15).

traditions.text: A thematic link. The Lord's preface to the Doctrine and Covenants makes the claim of v. 45 a standing rule: what he has spoken “shall all be fulfilled,” whether by his own voice or by his servants'. Joshua reports that every promise to Israel came to pass; D&C 1:37–38 tells readers to search these commandments because their prophecies and promises will do the same.

David Kimhi (Radak) noticed that v. 7 promises Merari twelve towns from Reuben, Gad, and Zebulun, but his text named only Zebulun's four and Gad's four. Some copies, he says, had a corrected reading adding Reuben's four towns, but he had not seen the two verses in any old and accurate manuscript. He cites a responsum of Hai Gaon, head of the Babylonian academy, who answered that the towns are counted in Chronicles even if not here, which suggests the verses were absent from the gaon's books as well.

The Greek text adds four lines after v. 42 that the Hebrew lacks. Joshua finishes dividing the land, the people give him the town he asked for, Thamnasachar in the hill country of Ephraim, and he builds it and lives there (compare 19:49–50). Then he takes the stone knives with which he had circumcised the Israelites born in the desert (5:2–7) and lays them up in his town. The Greek returns to the knives at his burial (24:30–31).

Josephus says Joshua told the tribes to give the Levites thirty-eight cities, because they had already received ten in the land of the Amorites. His numbers match the chapter's own split: Golan, Beeshterah, and Reuben's and Gad's eight towns make exactly ten east of the Jordan (vv. 27, 36–39), so his figure fits a text that included Reuben's four towns, the ones Radak could not find.

Hebron was a refuge and a priests' town, but Judges 1:20 says Hebron was given to Caleb. Abaye answers from vv. 11–12: the priests got the city itself, and Caleb got its fields and villages. The same passage asks whether only six towns gave refuge and answers from Numbers 35:6 that all forty-eight did; the difference is that the six took in a slayer even if he arrived by chance, while the other forty-two sheltered only one who came there on purpose.

The Mishnah fixes the shape of the Levites' “suburbs” (vv. 2–42): two thousand cubits around each town, the inner thousand left open and the outer thousand for fields and vineyards. Neither belt could be turned into the other, and no open land could be built over. Houses and fields in these towns also kept the Levites' special right of redemption at any time (Leviticus 25:32–34), and the sages extended it to any house in a Levite town, whoever owned it.

Rashi identifies “the rest of the children of Kohath” (v. 5) as the descendants of Moses and of Kohath's other sons Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, who were Levites but not priests. He notes that Almon (v. 18) appears in Chronicles as Alemeth, and he gives the measure of each town's pasture land as two thousand cubits on every side.

Origen observes that even the Levites, who live from Israel's tithes, receive their towns by lot, so that the division would come from providence and not from human choice. He follows the order of the lots, with Kohath first in honor as in the camp of Numbers, and then reads the spread of priestly towns through every quarter of the land as a picture of the age to come. The saints, he suggests, will be given their places in heaven in an order like that of the stars.
traditions.cite: Homilies on Joshua 25.1–4 (paraphrased from Bruce's translation)

traditions.text: Augustine asks how v. 43 can say God gave “all the land” when nations remained. He answers that the survivors were left as tributaries and as a test, and that the full extent of the promise was reached under Solomon. On v. 44, that no enemy stood before them, he suggests the statement treats the tribes as a single army before the land was divided, since Dan later struggled for its territory (19:47).

Eusebius locates the priests' town of Anathoth (v. 18) at the third milestone from Jerusalem and calls it the home of Jeremiah the prophet. His entries for Hebron, Shechem, and Golan likewise mark them as Levite towns and refuges, so a reader in Roman Palestine could walk from this chapter to places still inhabited in his day.

22.overview:
Joshua praises Reuben, Gad, and half Manasseh for keeping their promise, blesses them, and sends them home across the Jordan with a charge to serve the LORD and a share of the spoil. On the way they build a great altar by the river. The western tribes hear of it and gather at Shiloh for war. Phinehas the priest and ten princes cross over and accuse them of rebellion, citing Peor and Achan. The eastern tribes swear by “the LORD God of gods” that the altar is a copy, built as a witness and never meant for sacrifice. Phinehas accepts the answer, the war is called off, and the altar is named a witness.

The quarrel is really about who belongs to Israel. The eastern tribes fear that one day the western tribes will tell their children that the Jordan is a border and “ye have no part in the LORD” (v. 25).

historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Joshua's lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th century BC, drawing on older sources.

historicalContext.text: After the allotment, while the tabernacle stood at Shiloh (v. 12): about 1400 BC by the reckoning from 1 Kings 6:1; many scholars prefer the late 13th or 12th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Shiloh; Geliloth (KJV “the borders”) of the Jordan, on the Canaan side (v. 10); the land of Gilead east of the river.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Numbers 32 and Joshua 1:12–18 (the eastern tribes' promise); Deuteronomy 12:5–14 (one place of sacrifice).

22.hermeneutics:
A Jewish community in exile once negotiated over an altar outside the chosen place. In the 5th century BC Jewish soldiers at Elephantine, on Egypt's southern border, kept a temple of their God with an altar. After it was destroyed in 410 BC they wrote to the governor of Judah asking leave to rebuild and to offer meal offerings, incense, and burnt offerings as before. The surviving memorandum of the reply allows rebuilding and names only meal offering and incense; a fragmentary petition adds that sheep, oxen, and goats would not be offered there as burnt offerings. An altar outside the center could be accepted if it carried no animal sacrifice. The eastern tribes make the same promise in vv. 26–29: this altar is “not for burnt offerings, nor for sacrifices.”

The fear in vv. 16–19 also had a later form. When the kingdom split, Jeroboam I set up a calf at Dan, on Israel's northern border, so that his people need not go up to Jerusalem (1 Kings 12:28–30). Avraham Biran's excavations at Tel Dan uncovered a large raised platform of dressed stone, a cultic high place that he attributed to Jeroboam's time, later enlarged. A border sanctuary that drew people away from the central altar was a real danger in Israel's history. Readers who knew Dan and Bethel would hear the anger at Shiloh as reasonable, and the eastern tribes' oath as a promise not to become what Jeroboam later built.

A great altar by the Jordan; Israel gathers for war

The oath and answer: a witness, not a rival

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the chapter moves in sequence from dismissal to crisis to resolution, carried by repeated key words.

rows.text: Faithful service rewarded; the tribes sent home

notes: **The charge in counted words:** “altar” occurs 12 times in the Hebrew. “Turn from following the LORD” comes four times (vv. 16, 18, 23, 29), “rebel” five times (vv. 16, 18, 19 twice, 29), and the noun and verb for “trespass” seven times (vv. 16, 20, 22, 31).

**The answer in one word:** “witness” (*ed*) comes only in the defense and the naming (vv. 27, 28, 34). The KJV adds the name “Ed” in v. 34; the Hebrew reads only that they called the altar, “for it is a witness.”
**Pattern:** the altar is a *tavnit*, a copy (v. 28), the word used for the tabernacle's heavenly pattern in Exodus 25:9, 40.

With the land divided (21:43–45), the book turns to farewells. Chapter 22 releases the eastern tribes from their service (1:12–18), and Joshua's last speeches follow (chs. 23–24). The worry of v. 25, that the Jordan might become a border of faith, stands just before Joshua's two calls to the whole people to stay loyal.

**Backward and forward:** Phinehas, hero of Peor (Numbers 25:7–13), now turns aside a war with words, and v. 20 recalls Achan (7:1). The altar as a witness echoes the heap of Galeed, where Jacob and Laban made a cairn the witness between them (Genesis 31:47–48).

traditions.text: The Latter-day Saint edition links Joshua's charge to serve the LORD with all the heart and soul (v. 5) to D&C 4:2, which asks those who “embark in the service of God” to serve him with heart, might, mind, and strength. It links the altar's name, a witness that the LORD is God (v. 34), to the opening of D&C 76, where heaven and earth are told to rejoice because the Lord is God and beside him there is no Savior.

The Greek translators read the place-name Geliloth (v. 10) as Galaad, Gilead, and so put the altar on the Gilead side of the Jordan. At the end Joshua, not the eastern tribes, names the altar, declaring that it is a testimony among them that the LORD is their God. The Hebrew of v. 34 lacks a name, and the Greek supplies a speaker instead.

In Josephus the eastern tribes build the altar “as a monument to posterity” of their kinship with those across the river. It is Joshua, Eleazar, and the senate who hold back the armed tribes and insist on an embassy first. Phinehas threatens that if the land beyond the Jordan hinders the tribes' faith, Israel can divide the land again and leave Gilead for pasture, and when the answer comes Joshua offers sacrifices of thanksgiving because no kin blood will be shed.

This retelling makes the eastern tribes guilty. They really offered sacrifices and made priests for their sanctuary, and their defense is that their children might otherwise drift away. Joshua answers that if they had taught their sons the law day and night, no sanctuary made with hands would have been needed, and orders them to tear it down. Israel offers a thousand rams for them and they destroy the altar, fasting and weeping, after which Joshua sets up the tabernacle at Shiloh, where Eleazar answers inquirers by the Urim and Thummim.

Why would Israel go to war over an altar (v. 12)? Rashi answers that private altars were forbidden once the tabernacle stood at Shiloh. The Mishnah sets out the periods: private altars were allowed at Gilgal, forbidden at Shiloh, allowed again at Nob and Gibeon after Shiloh fell, and forbidden for good once the temple stood in Jerusalem. On that reckoning the eastern tribes built at exactly the time when sacrifice away from the tabernacle was banned.

Joshua tells the departing tribes to divide the spoil with their brothers (v. 8). Rashi offers two readings: the brothers are the other eastern tribesmen, or they are the men who stayed home east of the Jordan to guard the towns, wives, and children. On the second reading those who never crossed still share the spoil. It is the same rule David later fixed for those who stayed by the baggage: “they shall part alike” (1 Samuel 30:24).

Heretics, the midrash says, asked Rabbi Simlai about v. 22, where three names of God (El, Elohim, YHWH) are spoken twice, as if three gods were invoked. He answered that the verb is singular, “he knoweth,” not “they know.” His students wanted a better answer, and he told them the three are names of one God, as a person might say “Basileus, Augustus, Caesar” of one emperor.

Rashi calls v. 34 one of Scripture's shortened verses: a word has to be supplied, so that the tribes called the altar “Witness,” for it is a witness between them. The KJV, following the same reasoning, prints the name Ed in italics. On v. 24 he explains the tribes' fear: when their children came to sacrifice at Shiloh, others might mock them and ask what they had to do with the LORD.

Origen reads Reuben, the firstborn, and his companions as the righteous of the former people of the circumcision, who received their inheritance first. Their altar is not a rival but an imitation, a figure of the true altar where Jesus dwells and where the true sacrifices are offered. The two groups are finally made one flock under one shepherd.
traditions.cite: Homilies on Joshua 26.2–3 (paraphrased from Bruce's translation)

traditions.text: Augustine stops on a plural in his Latin text of v. 27, which speaks of sacrifices “of salvations.” He grants that the word can be used of offerings, but warns that Christ alone is the Savior of his body, so the plural should not be pressed into speaking of many saviors. The question shows a Latin reader working phrase by phrase through the tribes' defense.

23.overview:
Long after the wars have ended, Joshua, now old, calls together Israel's elders, heads, judges, and officers. He reminds them that the LORD fought for them and has already allotted the land still held by the nations. They must keep the law of Moses without turning aside, must not mention or swear by the nations' gods, and must cleave to the LORD; then one of them will chase a thousand. If they cleave instead to the nations that remain and marry among them, the LORD will stop driving those nations out, and they will become snares and traps until Israel perishes from the good land.

The speech turns the promise of 21:45 around. Not one good thing has failed (v. 14), and for that very reason every evil thing the LORD threatened will also come if Israel breaks the covenant (v. 15).

historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. The Talmud credits Joshua, with the account of his death added by Eleazar and Phinehas; many scholars see the book as part of a larger history compiled in the 7th–6th century BC.

historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Joshua's lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th century BC, drawing on older sources.

historicalContext.text: “A long time after” the land had rest (v. 1), near the end of Joshua's life at 110 (24:29). Josephus puts it twenty years after the altar episode; by 1 Kings 6:1 reckoning, about 1380 BC.

historicalContext.text: Israel's leaders (v. 2), and through them every later generation tempted by the gods of its neighbors.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts

23.hermeneutics:
In the ancient Near East an oath named the gods who guaranteed it. Old Babylonian sale contracts end with the parties swearing by the name of the gods and the king; one from the reign of Samsu-iluna, Hammurabi's son, names Marduk, Gula, and the king himself. To swear by a god was to make him the witness and enforcer of one's dealings. Verse 7 shuts that door completely: Israel is not to mention the names of their gods, nor “cause to swear by them.” A village that did business with its Canaanite neighbors would meet these oaths constantly, and Joshua treats the mere use of the names as the first step toward serving and bowing (v. 7).

Marriage between ruling houses was how ancient states sealed alliances. After the long war between Egypt and the Hittites, Ramesses II married a daughter of the Hittite king Hattusili III, who arrived in Egypt in his 34th year (about 1245 BC); the Hittite side insisted she be a principal wife, and the marriage was commemorated on a stela at Abu Simbel. Verse 12 forbids Israel to “cleave” to the remaining nations by intermarriage, using the same verb as v. 8, “cleave unto the LORD.” Marriage meant alliance, and alliance meant sharing gods. Solomon later did exactly this, beginning with Pharaoh's daughter, and his wives “turned away his heart after other gods” (1 Kings 3:1; 11:1–4).

The LORD fought for you and will finish the work
Keep the law; no oaths by their gods; cleave to the LORD
One shall chase a thousand: love the LORD
Intermarriage and its cost: snares, scourges, thorns
Every good word kept, every threatened evil sure

structure.summary: No strong pattern; the speech moves from what the LORD has done to what Israel must do, and closes with the threat.

rows.text: What the LORD has done and will do

notes: **Cleave:** the verb comes twice, for the two loyalties on offer: to the LORD (v. 8) or to the remnant of the nations (v. 12).

**Good and good land:** “good” occurs five times in vv. 13–16. Three times it describes the land Israel may lose (vv. 13, 15, 16); twice it describes the LORD's words (vv. 14, 15), set against “all evil things” in v. 15.
**Not one thing failed:** v. 14 says it twice, with the verb “fall” used in 21:45. Threats of being driven from the land frame the close (vv. 13, 16).

The first of Joshua's two farewells. Chapter 23 is addressed to the leaders, has no place-name, and looks ahead to danger; chapter 24 gathers all the tribes at Shechem, retells the past, and ends in a covenant. The image of the nations as “thorns in your eyes” picks up Moses' warning in Numbers 33:55.

**Forward:** Judges opens by carrying out v. 13. The angel at Bochim says the LORD will not drive the nations out and they will be thorns and snares (Judges 2:1–3), and Judges 2:20–23 says the nations Joshua left were kept to test Israel. David's charge to Solomon begins with Joshua's words, “I go the way of all the earth” (1 Kings 2:2).

traditions.text: Lehi, near death, uses Joshua's phrase of v. 14: in a few more days, he says, “I go the way of all the earth.” Like Joshua, he speaks to his family about a land given under covenant, consecrated to those the Lord brings there, which will be blessed while they keep the commandments and lost to them if they do not (2 Nephi 1:7, 20). The Church's footnote to v. 14 points to this verse.

The Lord tells Nephi that if his descendants rebel, the Lamanites will be a scourge to them, “to stir them up in the ways of remembrance.” The idea matches v. 13 and Judges 2:22: a neighboring people left in the land becomes the means of testing a covenant people. The Church's footnotes to v. 13 cite 1 Nephi 2:24 and 3 Nephi 20:28, where the risen Jesus applies the same word, scourge, to the Gentiles in the land; 2 Nephi 5:25 repeats Nephi's warning.

Jacob closes his account of the allegory of the olive tree by urging his people to “cleave unto God as he cleaveth unto you.” It takes the command of v. 8 and makes it mutual: God already cleaves to his people, and his arm of mercy is stretched out while it is still day. The Church's footnote to v. 8 points to this verse.

Josephus says Joshua settled at Shechem after the altar crisis and, twenty years later, very old, called the leading men of the cities, the officers, the senate, and as many of the people as he could gather. He reminded them how far God had raised them from a low estate to glory and plenty, and told them that God would remain their friend through nothing but their piety, a charge he wanted them to remember after his death. Josephus runs chs. 23 and 24 together into this one speech and passes over the covenant ceremony at Shechem.

This early rabbinic chronicle of biblical history gives Joshua twenty-eight years as Israel's leader, and so puts the “long time” of v. 1 near the end of that span. It goes straight from Joshua's leadership to his death and Eleazar's in the same period, then counts the judges who followed. Josephus, working independently, gives Joshua twenty-five years of rule after Moses.

Rashi reads the images of v. 13 as military ones. The word KJV renders “scourges” he takes from a root meaning to roam about, so the nations will prowl around Israel to raid and plunder. The “thorns” he reads as camps that surround a person like a shield on three sides, comparing Ezekiel 23:24. On v. 4 he explains that Joshua's “I have divided unto you” means by lot, even for the nations not yet conquered.

David Kimhi reads “ye know in all your hearts” (v. 14) as an appeal to reflect. Set your mind on all the good that has come, he paraphrases, and you will see that it could not have happened by chance, only by the intention of one who promised it to you. Because not one word failed, Israel can recognize that everything came from him. He also reads the verb “shall chase” in v. 10 as a future verb standing for a past, so Joshua points to what one Israelite has already done.

Tertullian takes up the ban on naming other gods, quoting it from Exodus 23:13 as v. 7 restates it. He grants that Christians must say things like “the temple of Aesculapius” in daily speech; what the law forbids is calling such beings gods. The oath is the danger: to swear by Hercules, even from habit, is to honor him, for no one swears by a name he holds as nothing. He adds that keeping silent when a pagan binds you by his gods is no better, since silence affirms their majesty.

Augustine comments on Joshua's “I am going the way of all the earth” (v. 14). The phrase means death, he says, and it is no surprise that Joshua speaks of the end he shares with everyone on earth; the return to God that follows death belongs only to those whose lives have deserved it. David uses the same words to Solomon (1 Kings 2:2), and Augustine's reading fits both deathbeds.

24.overview:
Joshua gathers all the tribes at Shechem and speaks for the LORD, retelling Israel's story in God's own voice: Terah's family serving other gods beyond the River, the call of Abraham, Egypt and the sea, the Amorites, Balaam, Jericho, and a land they did not labor for. Then he puts the choice: serve the LORD, or choose this day the gods of the fathers or of the Amorites; he and his house will serve the LORD. The people insist they will serve him. Joshua warns they cannot, for he is holy and jealous, and they insist again. Joshua makes a covenant, writes the words in the book of the law, and sets up a great stone as witness. Then come three burials: Joshua, Joseph's bones, and Eleazar.

The choice reaches back to Israel's own beginnings. The gods to be put away are first of all the ones “your fathers served” (vv. 2, 14–15).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named, though v. 26 says Joshua “wrote these words in the book of the law of God.” The Talmud credits Joshua, with his death added by Eleazar and Phinehas; many scholars see a larger history compiled in the 7th–6th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Joshua's lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); many scholars date its final form to the 7th–6th century BC, drawing on older sources.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: The end of Joshua's life, at 110 (v. 29): about 1380 BC by the reckoning from 1 Kings 6:1; many scholars prefer the 12th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Shechem, between Mounts Ebal and Gerizim, at “the sanctuary of the LORD” under an oak (v. 26). The Septuagint reads Shiloh. Burials at Timnath-serah, Shechem, and the hill of Phinehas in Ephraim.

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Judges 2:6–9 (Joshua's death and burial retold); Genesis 35:2–4 (Jacob puts away foreign gods at Shechem); Genesis 50:25 and Exodus 13:19 (Joseph's bones).

24.hermeneutics:
The two cities of Terah's story were the great centers of the moon god. Ur, where the family began (Genesis 11:31), had the temple of Nanna, the Sumerian moon god, beside its ziggurat. Harran, where Terah stopped and died, had the temple of Sin, the same god under his Akkadian name, rebuilt as late as the 6th century BC by the Babylonian king Nabonidus, whose mother served there. When v. 2 says Israel's fathers “served other gods” beyond the River, a hearer would think of real cults in real places. Israel's covenant does not begin with a people raised on the true God. It begins with a family that had to leave its gods behind, and v. 14 asks each generation to do the same.

Shechem already had a temple. In 1926 Ernst Sellin uncovered a massive fortress temple at Tell Balata, and in front of it stood a great limestone standing stone, the largest found in the land. Lawrence Stager has argued that the building remained in use into Iron Age I and is the “house of the god Berith” (“lord of the covenant”) of Judges 9:46, where Abimelech's story is set. Some scholars have suggested that the standing stone could be Joshua's “great stone” (v. 26) and the “pillar” of Judges 9:6. The identification remains a possibility, not a consensus. Either way, Joshua renews the covenant at a city where covenant gods were worshiped, and within a generation Shechem's own covenant shrine belongs to Baal (Judges 9:4).

notes: **Serve:** the Hebrew verb *avad* occurs 16 times in the chapter, 14 of them in the dialogue of vv. 14–24. Each round of the exchange ends with the people saying it again.
**Beyond the River:** the phrase comes four times (vv. 2, 3, 14, 15), tying the call to choose back to the fathers' gods. KJV renders the River (the Euphrates) as “the flood.”
**Witness:** the people are witnesses against themselves (v. 22, twice), and the stone is a witness because “it hath heard” (v. 27, twice).

The book's last scene. Chapter 23 warned the leaders; chapter 24 binds the whole people by covenant and then closes three lives, the leader, the patriarch whose bones came out of Egypt, and the priest. Verse 31 hands the story to the elders who outlived Joshua, the point where Judges takes it up.

**Backward and forward:** at the same Shechem oak Jacob buried his household's foreign gods (Genesis 35:4), and Joseph's bones rest in the field Jacob bought there (Genesis 33:19). Judges 2:6–9 repeats Joshua's death and burial, and Judges 9 returns to Shechem's pillar and temple.

traditions.text: Mormon explains why the Nephite judges could not punish Korihor for his teaching: there was no law against a man's belief, for, he writes, the scripture says, “Choose ye this day, whom ye will serve.” He reads v. 15 as a principle of law. Serving God was a person's privilege, and unbelief was not a crime, while murder, theft, and adultery were.

The same call appears long before Joshua in the Restoration account of Enoch. The Lord sends Enoch to preach with the words, “Choose ye this day, to serve the Lord God who made you.” Joshua's challenge at Shechem becomes one instance of a call God has issued since the earliest generations.

Verse 2 says only that Terah and his fathers “served other gods.” The Book of Abraham fills in the picture: Abraham's fathers had turned to the gods of Elkenah, Libnah, Mahmackrah, Korash, and Pharaoh, and tried to sacrifice Abraham himself. Terah repented for a time during a famine, but once settled in Haran he “turned again unto his idolatry.” The Church's footnotes link v. 2 to Abraham 2:5 and v. 14 to Abraham 1:5–7.

A thematic link. At the waters of Mormon, Alma invites believers to be baptized “as a witness before him” that they have covenanted to serve God and keep his commandments. At Shechem the people are their own witnesses that they have chosen to serve the LORD (v. 22). In both, serving God is the content of the covenant and the people's own act is its witness.

The Greek text sets the assembly and covenant at Shiloh, before the tabernacle, not Shechem (vv. 1, 25), while still burying Joseph at Shechem. After Joshua's burial it adds that the stone knives he used to circumcise Israel at Gilgal were put in the tomb with him and remain there “unto this day.” It closes with lines the Hebrew lacks: Israel carries the ark about among them, Phinehas succeeds Eleazar, and the people turn to Astarte and are given into the hand of Eglon of Moab, the opening of Judges 3.

Like the Septuagint, this retelling places the covenant at Shiloh, on the 16th day of the third month, near the feast of Weeks. God's history begins with one rock out of which Abraham and Nahor were hewn (Isaiah 51:1–2), and Abraham's vision of Genesis 15 becomes a revelation of the place of fire for the wicked and torches of light for the righteous. The people answer, “The Lord is our God, and him only will we serve,” and celebrate for twenty-eight days.

Pseudo-Philo has Israel lament Joshua as “the wing of this swift eagle” and bury him with their own hands. The Talmud tells the opposite story. The hill Gaash (v. 30) means “quaking,” Rav says, because the mountain raged to kill the people for failing to eulogize Joshua properly, and anyone slow to mourn a sage deserves the same.

Josephus gives Joshua's 110 years as forty with Moses, learning, and twenty-five as commander after him, and praises his wisdom, eloquence, and courage. He was buried at Timnath in Ephraim. Eleazar died about the same time, leaving the high priesthood to Phinehas, and his tomb was at Gabatha.

Why bury Joseph at Shechem? Rabbi Hama son of Rabbi Hanina answers that Joseph's brothers took him from Shechem (Genesis 37:12–28), so to Shechem Israel returned what had been lost. The Talmud also notes that Exodus 13:19 credits Moses with carrying the bones while v. 32 credits the children of Israel, and concludes that whoever finishes a deed gets the credit for it.

What did Joshua write “in the book of the law” (v. 26)? Two rabbis disagree: one says the last eight verses of Deuteronomy, on Moses' death; the other says the chapter on the cities of refuge, which Joshua copied into his own book. Rashi adds the Targum's reading that Joshua laid his words up beside the Torah scroll, and identifies the oak as the one under which Jacob buried the strange gods at Shechem.

Augustine reads the people's confidence in v. 21 as boasting: Joshua had warned that they could not serve a holy God, and they relied on themselves instead of seeking grace, as Romans later teaches. The stone that “hath heard” (v. 27) is set up visibly, he says, but must be understood spiritually, and the covenant points ahead to the new covenant.

Eusebius says Joshua's tomb was still pointed out in his day near the village of Thamna, north of Mount Gaas. He also places the oak of Shechem, where Abimelech was made king, in the outskirts of Neapolis toward the tomb of Joseph, so that the oak, the stone, and the grave of v. 32 were all remembered as one neighborhood.

In his memorial of Paula's pilgrimage, Jerome says she visited the tombs of Joshua and Eleazar in the hill country of Ephraim, facing each other, Joshua's at Timnath-serah north of Gaash and Eleazar's on the hill of Phinehas. She was surprised that the man who divided the whole land had chosen such rough and rocky ground for himself.
